Stress testing is not a screening tool for Marfan-related cardiovascular complications. Coronary artery disease is not the main health maintenance issue in this patient; aortic surveillance is.

questions.teaching_point: In Marfan syndrome, ongoing outpatient care should prioritize periodic aortic root surveillance, usually with echocardiography.

questions.vignette: A 3-week-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic because he has not passed stool for 4 days and has had progressive abdominal distension. He fed well in the first week of life, but his parents report that he has had intermittent vomiting and very small, foul-smelling stools after rectal stimulation at home. He was born at term, and there is no family history of bowel disease. On exam, he appears uncomfortable with a moderately distended abdomen. Rectal exam produces a gush of stool and gas followed by temporary relief of distension.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is most appropriate as the initial study to support the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Anorectal manometry
Contrast enema
Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan
Upper gastrointestinal series
Abdominal ultrasound

questions.rationale: Contrast enema is the most appropriate initial study when Hirschsprung disease is suspected. It may show a transition zone between the dilated proximal colon and the narrow distal aganglionic segment, which supports the diagnosis and helps guide further evaluation. Rectal suction biopsy is the definitive diagnostic test because it demonstrates absence of ganglion cells, but the question asks for the best initial study to support the suspected diagnosis, making contrast enema the correct choice.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Anorectal manometry can demonstrate absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex and may be used in older infants or children, but it is not the preferred initial study in a symptomatic neonate with suspected Hirschsprung disease.
A HIDA scan assesses biliary excretion and is used for suspected biliary atresia or other causes of neonatal cholestasis, not neonatal bowel obstruction or Hirschsprung disease.
An upper gastrointestinal series is used to evaluate malrotation, volvulus, or proximal intestinal obstruction, which does not match this infant’s presentation of distal functional obstruction.

Abdominal ultrasound is useful for conditions such as pyloric stenosis or intussusception, but it does not evaluate distal colonic aganglionosis and would not support the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected Hirschsprung disease, contrast enema is the best initial supportive study, while rectal suction biopsy is the definitive diagnostic test.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man is evaluated in clinic after an abdominal ultrasound obtained for intermittent right flank discomfort incidentally shows a 4.8-cm solid mass in the upper pole of the left kidney. He has no fever, dysuria, or weight loss. He has a 25-pack-year smoking history and well-controlled hypertension. Physical examination is unremarkable. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirms a 5.0-cm enhancing renal mass confined to the kidney with no renal vein invasion or metastatic disease. He is otherwise healthy and asks what should be done next.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Start neoadjuvant sunitinib before definitive therapy
Perform percutaneous needle biopsy before any intervention
Begin active surveillance with repeat imaging in 6 months
Refer for partial nephrectomy with renal-preserving intent
Schedule radical nephrectomy as the initial treatment

questions.rationale: This patient has a localized, enhancing renal mass consistent with renal cell carcinoma, measuring 5.0 cm and confined to the kidney (clinical stage T1b). In a healthy patient with a localized tumor, the preferred management is surgical resection, with partial nephrectomy favored when technically feasible because it preserves renal function while providing oncologic control. A biopsy is usually not required before definitive surgery when imaging strongly suggests RCC in a surgically fit patient. Radical nephrectomy is generally reserved for tumors not amenable to nephron-sparing surgery or more extensive disease. Surveillance is more appropriate for small renal masses in selected older or frail patients, not for a healthy adult with a 5-cm lesion. Neoadjuvant targeted therapy is not standard initial treatment for localized RCC.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Sunitinib is a systemic therapy used in advanced or metastatic RCC, not as neoadjuvant treatment for a localized renal mass that is already resectable.

Percutaneous biopsy can be useful when imaging is indeterminate or when results would change management, but a classic enhancing localized renal mass in a surgical candidate is typically treated definitively without preoperative biopsy.

Active surveillance is mainly considered for small renal masses, significant comorbidity, or limited life expectancy. This patient is healthy and has a 5-cm enhancing lesion, making immediate definitive treatment more appropriate.

Radical nephrectomy is not the preferred initial approach for a localized 5-cm tumor when partial nephrectomy is feasible. Nephron-sparing surgery is favored to preserve renal function in appropriate candidates.

questions.teaching_point: For a localized enhancing renal mass in a fit adult, partial nephrectomy is preferred when feasible to preserve renal function.

questions.vignette: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus returns for routine follow-up in clinic. He has been taking metformin 1000 mg twice daily for 8 months, following a calorie-controlled diet, and walking most days of the week. His A1c today is 8.4%. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 78 mL/min/1.73 m2, he has no history of pancreatitis, and his body mass index is 34 kg/m2. After discussing options for additional therapy, he says he would most like a medication that can help with both glycemic control and weight loss.
questions.lead_in: Which medication is the best next step to add to his current regimen?

answer_choices.text: Pioglitazone
Glipizide
Insulin glargine
Empagliflozin
Liraglutide

questions.rationale: Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist and is a good add-on to metformin in type 2 diabetes when additional A1c lowering and weight loss are desired. In this patient, it is especially appropriate because he is obese and specifically wants a medication that can aid with weight loss. Although empagliflozin is also an appropriate add-on option and can promote some weight loss, GLP-1 receptor agonists generally produce greater weight reduction and are a strong choice when weight loss is a priority.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pioglitazone can improve glycemic control, but it commonly causes weight gain and fluid retention, making it a poor match for a patient trying to lose weight.
Glipizide can reduce A1c, but sulfonylureas are associated with hypoglycemia and weight gain, so they are less desirable when weight loss is a goal.

Insulin glargine lowers glucose effectively but is not the best next step here because the patient is not severely hyperglycemic, does not have catabolic symptoms, and is specifically seeking an option that may also help with weight loss.

Empagliflozin is a reasonable add-on therapy after metformin and may cause modest weight loss, but liraglutide is preferred here because the patient specifically wants a medication that helps with weight loss and GLP-1 receptor agonists generally have a stronger weight-loss effect.

questions.teaching_point: When type 2 diabetes remains above goal on metformin, a GLP-1 receptor agonist is an excellent add-on option for patients with obesity who want improved glycemic control and weight loss.

questions.vignette: A 46-year-old woman comes to clinic for persistently elevated blood pressure despite taking amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. She reports mild muscle cramps but no chest pain, palpitations, or headaches. Blood pressure is 162/98 mm Hg. Basic metabolic panel shows potassium 3.1 mEq/L and bicarbonate 31 mEq/L. Creatinine is normal. She does not use licorice, steroids, or over-the-counter decongestants. On repeat measurement, her blood pressure remains elevated.
questions.lead_in: Which outpatient diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to evaluate for the suspected cause of her hypertension and hypokalemia?

answer_choices.text: Plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity to calculate an aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Renal artery Doppler ultrasonography
Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
Plasma fractionated metanephrines
24-hour urinary free cortisol level

questions.rationale: This patient has hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, which strongly suggests primary aldosteronism. The appropriate initial outpatient screening test is the plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity, used to calculate the aldosterone-to-renin ratio. An elevated ratio indicates autonomous aldosterone production and prompts confirmatory testing. Because potassium depletion and several antihypertensive medications can affect the result, potassium should be corrected and medication effects considered when interpreting the test.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Renal artery Doppler ultrasonography evaluates renovascular hypertension, which is a possible secondary cause of hypertension but does not specifically address the classic combination of hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis seen here.
The low-dose dexamethasone suppression test screens for Cushing syndrome, not primary aldosteronism.

Plasma fractionated metanephrines are used to evaluate pheochromocytoma, which typically presents with episodic headache, diaphoresis, palpitations, and labile blood pressure rather than persistent hypertension with hypokalemia.

A 24-hour urinary free cortisol level is a screening test for Cushing syndrome. Although Cushing syndrome can cause hypertension, this patient’s hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is more characteristic of primary aldosteronism.

questions.teaching_point: In adults with hypertension plus hypokalemia, the first outpatient screening test for primary aldosteronism is the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, with attention to potassium status and medication effects.

questions.vignette: A 44-year-old woman is seen for preoperative evaluation before a planned laparoscopic hysterectomy for heavy menstrual bleeding. For 2 years, she has had progressively heavier menses with clots and pelvic pressure. She has no intermenstrual bleeding, no postcoital bleeding, and no weight loss. She is otherwise healthy. Pelvic exam shows a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus that is mobile and mildly tender. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a uterus enlarged by several well-circumscribed, hypoechoic intramural masses that distort the contour of the uterine body; the ovaries are normal.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this patient’s symptoms and imaging findings?

answer_choices.text: Endometrial polyp
Uterine leiomyoma
Adenomyosis
Pelvic inflammatory disease
Endometrial carcinoma

questions.rationale: Uterine leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumors that commonly cause heavy regular menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and an enlarged, irregularly contoured uterus. Ultrasound typically shows well-circumscribed, hypoechoic uterine masses. In this patient, the chronic heavy menses with clots, pressure symptoms, firm irregular uterus, and classic intramural masses on ultrasound are most consistent with fibroids. The absence of intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding makes an endometrial or cervical source less likely, and the normal ovaries support a uterine rather than adnexal process.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Endometrial polyps can cause abnormal uterine bleeding, often intermenstrual bleeding, but they are focal intrauterine lesions rather than multiple intramural masses distorting the uterine contour.
Adenomyosis can cause heavy, painful menses and a boggy, enlarged uterus, but it more often causes diffuse uterine enlargement rather than multiple well-circumscribed intramural masses on ultrasound.

Pelvic inflammatory disease typically presents with pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, fever, discharge, or adnexal tenderness, not a chronic pattern of heavy cyclic bleeding with a firm irregular uterus and fibroid-appearing ultrasound findings.

Endometrial carcinoma is more concerning with postmenopausal bleeding, persistent abnormal uterine bleeding, or risk factors such as obesity and unopposed estrogen; this patient’s presentation is more typical of a benign myometrial mass.

questions.teaching_point: Leiomyomas classically cause heavy menstrual bleeding and a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus with well-circumscribed hypoechoic masses on ultrasound.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old man is brought to the operating room for urgent decompressive craniectomy after a severe motor vehicle collision. Earlier in the emergency department, head CT showed a right subdural hematoma with a 9-mm midline shift. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated. Just before incision, his heart rate is 48/min, blood pressure is 198/96 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 99% on 40% FiO2. The anesthesia team notes that he becomes more bradycardic and hypertensive when the surgical drapes are placed.
questions.lead_in: Which immediate perioperative intervention is most appropriate to help reduce intracranial pressure and prevent secondary brain injury while definitive decompression is underway?

answer_choices.text: Start phenylephrine to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure
Increase end-tidal carbon dioxide to improve cerebral blood flow
Place the patient in the Trendelenburg position to improve cerebral perfusion
Administer hypertonic saline to lower intracranial pressure
Initiate nitrous oxide to reduce anesthetic requirements

questions.rationale: This patient has severe traumatic brain injury with radiographic mass effect and perioperative bradycardia plus hypertension, concerning for markedly elevated intracranial pressure. Hypertonic saline is an appropriate immediate temporizing therapy because it reduces cerebral edema and can lower intracranial pressure while the patient is being prepared for definitive surgical decompression. In the operating room, this should occur alongside other supportive measures such as maintaining oxygenation, avoiding hypotension, and targeting normocapnia.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Phenylephrine may be used to support blood pressure and cerebral perfusion pressure if hypotension develops, but it does not directly lower intracranial pressure. In a patient with signs of intracranial hypertension, osmotherapy is the more appropriate immediate temporizing measure.
Increasing carbon dioxide causes cerebral vasodilation, which increases cerebral blood flow and can worsen intracranial pressure. Normocapnia is generally preferred in severe traumatic brain injury.
Trendelenburg positioning increases venous congestion in the head and can worsen intracranial pressure. Head elevation is preferred when feasible to facilitate venous drainage.
Nitrous oxide increases cerebral blood flow and can raise intracranial pressure, so it should be avoided in severe traumatic brain injury or suspected intracranial hypertension.

questions.teaching_point: In severe traumatic brain injury with signs of intracranial hypertension, use temporizing measures that lower intracranial pressure, such as hypertonic saline, while avoiding interventions that increase cerebral blood flow or venous congestion.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man is admitted for sudden-onset severe chest pain that began while he was lifting a heavy box. He describes the pain as “tearing” and says it radiates to his back. He is diaphoretic and anxious. Blood pressure is 176/92 mm Hg in the right arm and 154/88 mm Hg in the left arm. Heart rate is 108/min. Examination shows a new early diastolic murmur best heard along the left sternal border. His creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. ECG shows nonspecific ST-T changes, and serial troponins are negative. The patient remains hemodynamically stable after initial pain control.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: CT angiography of the chest with contrast
Stress myocardial perfusion imaging
Transesophageal echocardiography
Coronary angiography
Chest radiograph

questions.rationale: CT angiography of the chest with contrast is the most appropriate next diagnostic study in a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected aortic dissection. This patient has several high-risk features, including abrupt tearing chest pain radiating to the back, inter-arm blood pressure difference, and a new diastolic murmur suggesting aortic regurgitation. CT angiography provides rapid, highly sensitive visualization of the aorta and helps define the extent of the dissection for urgent management planning.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Stress myocardial perfusion imaging is inappropriate because acute aortic dissection must be excluded first and exercise or pharmacologic stress could worsen the condition.

Transesophageal echocardiography is also useful for diagnosing aortic dissection, especially if the patient is unstable or cannot receive contrast. However, this patient is stable, making CT angiography the preferred confirmatory study in most inpatient settings.

Coronary angiography is used to evaluate acute coronary syndrome, but this presentation is more concerning for aortic dissection than myocardial ischemia, and invasive arterial instrumentation is not the first confirmatory test here.
Chest radiograph may show a widened mediastinum or pleural effusion, but it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to confirm the diagnosis and should not replace definitive vascular imaging.

questions.teaching_point: In a stable patient with suspected aortic dissection, CT angiography is the preferred confirmatory test; unstable patients may need transesophageal echocardiography instead.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is seen in a primary care clinic by his daughter for worsening headaches and intermittent confusion over the past 3 weeks. He slipped on ice and struck the left side of his head about 1 month ago, but he did not lose consciousness and did not seek care. Since then, he has become increasingly forgetful, has had two brief episodes of stumbling, and today reports mild right-hand clumsiness. He takes daily aspirin for coronary artery disease. In the office, he is awake and oriented but slower to answer questions than usual. Vital signs are normal. Neurologic exam shows mild right pronator drift and a slightly unsteady gait.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Send him to the emergency department for urgent noncontrast head CT; obtain neurosurgical consultation if imaging confirms hemorrhage or if symptoms worsen
Reassure the patient that postconcussive symptoms commonly last for several weeks and schedule routine follow-up
Order brain MRI as an outpatient because it is more sensitive than CT for chronic subdural blood
Arrange an outpatient noncontrast head CT within the next week and advise close follow-up unless symptoms worsen
Increase his aspirin dose to reduce the risk of transient ischemic attack

questions.rationale: This older adult has a classic presentation concerning for chronic subdural hematoma: minor head trauma several weeks earlier, followed by progressive headache, confusion, gait instability, and focal neurologic findings. The most appropriate next step is urgent emergency evaluation with noncontrast head CT because imaging is needed promptly to confirm intracranial bleeding. If a hemorrhage is found, neurosurgical consultation is indicated for possible drainage; urgent consultation is also warranted if neurologic status worsens. Waiting for outpatient imaging would be unsafe.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Postconcussive symptoms do not explain progressive confusion, gait disturbance, and focal neurologic deficits weeks after trauma in an older adult. This presentation is concerning for chronic subdural hematoma.
MRI can detect chronic subdural blood, but it should not delay urgent evaluation. Noncontrast head CT is the preferred initial test because it is rapid and readily available in this setting.
Outpatient imaging is too slow for a patient with progressive neurologic symptoms and focal deficits after head trauma. He needs immediate emergency evaluation.
Increasing aspirin would raise bleeding risk and does not address a presentation that is concerning for intracranial hemorrhage rather than ischemia.

questions.teaching_point: In an older adult with delayed, progressive headache, confusion, gait change, or focal deficits after even minor head trauma, urgent noncontrast head CT is needed to evaluate for chronic subdural hematoma, with neurosurgical involvement if hemorrhage is present.

questions.vignette: A 67-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring positive-pressure ventilation. Two hours after intubation, he becomes acutely restless and dyspneic. His blood pressure drops to 78/46 mm Hg, heart rate increases to 132/min, and oxygen saturation falls to 84% despite 100% FiO2. Examination shows absent breath sounds on the right, distended neck veins, and a trachea that appears slightly deviated to the left. The endotracheal tube is in the expected position and bilateral chest rise is now asymmetric.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

answer_choices.text: Administer intravenous furosemide for presumed flash pulmonary edema
Obtain an urgent portable chest radiograph before intervening
Increase positive-end expiratory pressure to improve oxygenation
Order CT angiography of the chest to evaluate for pulmonary embolism
Perform emergent needle decompression of the right chest followed by tube thoracostomy

questions.rationale: This patient has an acute tension pneumothorax after positive-pressure ventilation, suggested by sudden hypoxemia and hypotension, unilateral absent breath sounds, distended neck veins, and tracheal deviation. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and requires immediate decompression without waiting for imaging. Needle decompression provides rapid temporary relief, followed by definitive chest tube placement on the affected side.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Flash pulmonary edema typically causes diffuse crackles and bilateral infiltrates rather than unilateral absent breath sounds, neck vein distention, and tracheal deviation.
A chest radiograph may confirm the diagnosis in a stable patient, but imaging should not delay decompression in a hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected tension pneumothorax.
Increasing positive pressure can worsen intrathoracic pressure and further impair venous return, making tension pneumothorax more severe.

Pulmonary embolism can cause hypoxemia and shock, but it does not explain the unilateral absent breath sounds, asymmetric chest rise, or tracheal deviation in this unstable post-intubation patient. CT angiography would delay life-saving treatment.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected tension pneumothorax, immediate decompression is the priority; do not wait for confirmatory imaging in an unstable patient.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old woman comes to clinic for persistent worry. For the past 9 months, she has felt “on edge” about work performance, her children’s safety, and finances nearly every day. She has difficulty controlling the worry, trouble sleeping, muscle tension, and fatigue. She denies panic attacks, obsessive thoughts, trauma exposure, manic symptoms, or substance use. Her exam is normal except for mild tremulousness. Her primary care clinician explains that her symptoms are consistent with a disorder involving dysregulation of a key inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain.
questions.lead_in: Which neurotransmitter is most directly implicated in the pathophysiology of this disorder?

answer_choices.text: Glutamate
Acetylcholine
Dopamine
Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
Serotonin

questions.rationale: Generalized anxiety disorder is associated with reduced inhibitory signaling in the central nervous system, especially involving GABA. Many first-line treatments for anxiety disorders, including benzodiazepines, enhance GABA-A receptor activity, reflecting this pathophysiology.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Glutamate is the major excitatory neurotransmitter; while it may play a role in anxiety circuitry, generalized anxiety disorder is classically linked to impaired GABA-mediated inhibition.
Acetylcholine is primarily associated with neuromuscular transmission, autonomic function, and memory rather than the main inhibitory neurotransmitter deficit in generalized anxiety disorder.
Dopamine is more closely associated with reward, psychosis, and movement pathways than the core inhibitory neurotransmitter dysfunction implicated in generalized anxiety disorder.
Serotonin is involved in anxiety regulation and is a target of SSRIs, but the key inhibitory neurotransmitter classically implicated in generalized anxiety disorder is GABA.

questions.teaching_point: Generalized anxiety disorder is classically associated with decreased GABA-mediated inhibitory signaling in the CNS.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man comes to clinic 2 days after laparoscopic abdominal surgery. He reports mild shortness of breath and discomfort taking a deep breath because of incisional pain. He has been spending most of the day in bed and is using his prescribed opioid medication regularly. He denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, or productive cough. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. On exam, he is taking shallow breaths. Lung examination reveals decreased breath sounds and fine crackles at the right base that improve after several coached deep breaths and coughing.
questions.lead_in: Which historical and physical examination finding most strongly supports the cause of this patient’s symptoms?

answer_choices.text: Productive cough with purulent sputum and focal egophony
Recent postoperative shallow breathing with decreased basilar breath sounds that improve after deep inspiration
Fever with pleuritic chest pain and unilateral leg swelling
Sudden dyspnea with hemoptysis after a recent long-distance flight
Diffuse wheezing that worsens at night and improves with albuterol

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has postoperative atelectasis caused by shallow breathing, splinting from incisional pain, and relative immobility. The key history is recent surgery with opioid use and limited deep breathing, and the key physical finding is decreased basilar breath sounds with crackles that improve after coached deep breaths and coughing, which is typical of reversible alveolar collapse from poor ventilation. Mild dyspnea with normal oxygenation and no infectious or thromboembolic features also supports atelectasis rather than pneumonia or pulmonary embolism.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Productive cough, purulent sputum, and egophony suggest pneumonia. This patient lacks fever, sputum production, and focal signs of consolidation.
Fever, pleuritic chest pain, and unilateral leg swelling would raise concern for pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis, not postoperative atelectasis. This patient has no fever or leg findings.
Sudden dyspnea and hemoptysis after prolonged travel suggests pulmonary embolism, which is usually not associated with crackles that improve after deep breathing.

Diffuse nocturnal wheezing relieved by albuterol is more consistent with asthma. Atelectasis typically causes localized diminished breath sounds and improves with incentive-type maneuvers or coughing.

questions.teaching_point: Postoperative atelectasis is suggested by shallow breathing, immobility, and basilar breath sounds that improve with deep inspiration and coughing.

questions.vignette: A 9-year-old boy is brought for preoperative evaluation before planned resection of a cerebellar mass found on MRI after several months of morning headaches, vomiting, and unsteady gait. His parents report that he has also been "tilting" his head to one side to keep objects in view. On exam, he is alert with normal speech. He has broad-based gait, impaired rapid alternating movements, and horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze. Vital signs are normal.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding is most likely in this child?

answer_choices.text: Resting tremor that decreases with voluntary movement
Increased head circumference with bulging anterior fontanelle
Ptosis with miosis and anhidrosis on one side of the face
Papilledema
Hyperreflexia with ankle clonus

questions.rationale: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a common pediatric posterior fossa tumor. In this child, the combination of morning headaches, vomiting, and cerebellar signs suggests a mass causing obstructive hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure. Papilledema is a classic additional physical examination finding in increased intracranial pressure. The cerebellar findings in the vignette already indicate posterior fossa involvement, and papilledema best explains the associated headache and vomiting.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A resting tremor that decreases with voluntary movement is characteristic of parkinsonism, not a cerebellar tumor.
Increased head circumference with a bulging anterior fontanelle is a sign of elevated intracranial pressure in infants with open fontanelles, not in a 9-year-old child.
Ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis are features of Horner syndrome, which is not the expected finding with a cerebellar tumor or obstructive hydrocephalus.
Hyperreflexia with ankle clonus suggests an upper motor neuron or spinal cord process, which does not fit a cerebellar posterior fossa mass.

questions.teaching_point: Posterior fossa tumors in children commonly cause cerebellar signs such as ataxia and nystagmus and may also produce increased intracranial pressure with papilledema, morning headache, and vomiting.

questions.vignette: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department for intermittent episodes of severe crying and knee-flexing over the past 8 hours. Between episodes, he appears tired but consolable. His parents report three episodes of nonbilious vomiting and a stool that looked "dark and jelly-like." He had an upper respiratory infection 1 week ago. On examination, his temperature is 37.8 C (100.0 F), heart rate is 158/min, and blood pressure is 86/52 mm Hg. His abdomen is mildly distended, and he cries when it is palpated. During one episode, he draws his legs up and becomes pale.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding would be most consistent with this child's condition?

answer_choices.text: Bilious vomiting with a scaphoid abdomen and decreased bowel sounds
A palpable olive-like mass in the epigastrium
Right lower quadrant tenderness with involuntary guarding and rebound
A sausage-shaped abdominal mass in the right upper quadrant
Diffuse abdominal distension with delayed passage of meconium since birth

questions.rationale: This infant has intussusception, suggested by intermittent colicky abdominal pain, episodic leg-drawing, nonbilious vomiting, and currant jelly stool. A characteristic physical examination finding is a palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass, often in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, caused by telescoping of one bowel segment into another. The child can also appear lethargic between painful episodes.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Bilious vomiting with a scaphoid abdomen suggests malrotation with midgut volvulus or another obstructive process causing distal intestinal obstruction, not the classic presentation of intussusception.

A palpable olive-like epigastric mass is classic for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which typically causes progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting in a younger infant and does not cause currant jelly stools.

Right lower quadrant tenderness with guarding and rebound is more suggestive of appendicitis or peritonitis; appendicitis is uncommon at this age and does not typically present with currant jelly stool.

Diffuse abdominal distension with delayed passage of meconium since birth is more consistent with Hirschsprung disease, especially if associated with constipation and failure to thrive, rather than acute intermittent colicky pain.

questions.teaching_point: Intussusception in infants classically causes intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, lethargy, currant jelly stool, and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old woman is seen in clinic for fatigue and intermittent constipation. She has no history of kidney stones or fractures. She takes no calcium supplements and her only medication is lisinopril. She has had repeated outpatient labs over the past 6 months showing mild hypercalcemia, with total calcium 10.9-11.2 mg/dL, albumin normal, intact parathyroid hormone elevated, and creatinine normal. A 24-hour urine calcium is not low. Bone density testing shows osteopenia at the lumbar spine. She asks what the best next step in management is.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next management step?

answer_choices.text: Start cinacalcet therapy
Reassure her that no treatment or follow-up is needed
Begin loop diuretic therapy
Refer for parathyroidectomy
Start high-dose vitamin D and oral calcium supplementation

questions.rationale: This patient has primary hyperparathyroidism with persistent mild hypercalcemia, inappropriately elevated PTH, and evidence of skeletal involvement (osteopenia). In symptomatic patients or those with guideline-based indications such as reduced bone density, surgery is the definitive treatment and is the most appropriate next step in an outpatient setting.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cinacalcet can lower calcium in primary hyperparathyroidism, but it is generally used when surgery is not possible or not desired, not as the preferred definitive management in an otherwise appropriate surgical candidate.

Observation alone is reserved for selected asymptomatic patients without indications for surgery. This patient has persistent hypercalcemia and decreased bone density, so follow-up without intervention would be inappropriate.

Loop diuretics are not used chronically to treat primary hyperparathyroidism and can worsen volume depletion. They may transiently increase urinary calcium excretion but are not appropriate outpatient management here.
Vitamin D deficiency should be corrected if present, but high-dose calcium supplementation would worsen hypercalcemia and is not appropriate treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.teaching_point: Primary hyperparathyroidism is definitively treated with parathyroidectomy when patients have symptoms or complications such as low bone density, kidney stones, significant hypercalcemia, or reduced renal function.

questions.vignette: A 49-year-old man comes to the clinic for fatigue, decreased libido, and vague right upper quadrant discomfort. He reports that his skin has become darker over the past year despite no change in sun exposure. His father died of "liver disease" in his 50s. Examination shows mild hepatomegaly and bronze hyperpigmentation of the skin. Laboratory studies reveal ferritin 980 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 68%, and mildly elevated AST and ALT. Hepatitis B and C testing is negative.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

answer_choices.text: Order HFE genotyping to confirm hereditary hemochromatosis before starting treatment
Begin high-dose prednisone to reduce hepatic inflammation
Administer deferoxamine because this is the preferred initial treatment for all iron overload states
Begin therapeutic phlebotomy and monitor ferritin until iron stores normalize
Start oral iron supplementation and recheck blood counts in 3 months

questions.rationale: This patient has findings strongly suggestive of hereditary hemochromatosis, including fatigue, hypogonadal symptoms, hepatomegaly, bronze skin hyperpigmentation, elevated ferritin, and increased transferrin saturation. In a stable outpatient with suspected or confirmed hereditary hemochromatosis and no contraindication such as severe anemia, the initial treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy to remove excess iron and prevent complications such as cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and hypogonadism. Ferritin is followed serially to guide treatment toward iron depletion, and patients are also evaluated for complications and, when appropriate, HFE mutation testing.

distractor_rationales.explanation: HFE genotyping can help confirm the diagnosis, but treatment should not be delayed in a patient with a classic presentation and clear iron overload. Therapeutic phlebotomy is the initial treatment, provided hemoglobin is adequate.
Glucocorticoids do not treat hereditary hemochromatosis and would not reduce excess iron deposition.

Iron chelation is generally reserved for patients who cannot undergo phlebotomy, such as those with significant anemia or some transfusion-related iron overload states. It is not first-line for uncomplicated hereditary hemochromatosis.
Oral iron would worsen iron overload and is inappropriate in a patient with markedly elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation.

questions.teaching_point: Hereditary hemochromatosis is treated first-line with therapeutic phlebotomy, with ferritin monitoring and assessment for end-organ complications.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman comes to an outpatient clinic for contraception counseling. She had a copper IUD removed 2 months ago because of heavier menses and wants a method that is highly effective, requires little daily attention, and may make her periods lighter. She has migraines with aura, takes no medications, and smokes 5 cigarettes per day. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, BMI is 24 kg/m2, and urine pregnancy test is negative. She says she is certain she does not want pregnancy for several years and asks for the best option today.
questions.lead_in: Which contraceptive method is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?

answer_choices.text: Etonogestrel implant
Progestin-only pill
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection
Combined oral contraceptive pill
Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device

questions.rationale: The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device is the best choice because it is highly effective, long-acting, requires minimal adherence, and commonly decreases menstrual bleeding, which matches her desire for lighter periods after heavier bleeding with a copper IUD. It is also appropriate in a patient with migraine with aura, in whom estrogen-containing contraception should be avoided because of increased stroke risk. Her negative pregnancy test and desire for several years of contraception make same-day placement appropriate if there are no other contraindications.

distractor_rationales.explanation: The etonogestrel implant is highly effective and avoids estrogen, but it commonly causes irregular, unpredictable bleeding. Because she specifically wants lighter periods after prior problems with bleeding, this is less appropriate than a levonorgestrel IUD.

The progestin-only pill avoids estrogen and is safe with migraine with aura, but it requires strict daily timing and is less effective in typical use than long-acting reversible methods. It does not fit her request for minimal day-to-day attention.

Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is an effective progestin-only option, but it can cause irregular bleeding and may not satisfy her preference for lighter, more predictable menses. It is also less immediately reversible than an IUD and is not the best match for her goals.

Combined oral contraceptive pills contain estrogen and are contraindicated in patients with migraine with aura because of increased ischemic stroke risk. They also require daily adherence and are less ideal for someone seeking a low-maintenance method.

questions.teaching_point: In patients with migraine with aura, avoid estrogen-containing contraception; a levonorgestrel IUD is a strong long-acting option when lighter menses are desired.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: An 8-week-old infant is brought to an outpatient pediatric clinic because the parents have noticed a pale reflection in photographs of the baby’s right eye for the past 2 weeks. The infant is otherwise feeding well and has no fever or eye discharge. On exam, there is an abnormal white pupillary reflex in the right eye and a subtle strabismus. The anterior segment appears clear, and the red reflex is diminished on the affected side.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Prescribe topical antibiotic drops and reassess in 1 week
Order a plain orbital x-ray to evaluate for a calcified ocular lesion
Arrange urgent referral to pediatric ophthalmology and ocular oncology for prompt evaluation and treatment
Reassure the parents that this finding is a normal variant in infants
Schedule routine vision screening at the 12-month well-child visit

questions.rationale: This infant has leukocoria and strabismus, which are concerning for retinoblastoma and require urgent specialist evaluation. In an outpatient setting, the correct next step is immediate referral to pediatric ophthalmology/ocular oncology rather than watchful waiting or empiric treatment. Retinoblastoma is an ophthalmic emergency because prompt diagnosis and treatment are needed to preserve vision and reduce the risk of extraocular spread and metastatic disease.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Topical antibiotics may be appropriate for conjunctivitis, but this presentation lacks discharge, conjunctival injection, or eyelid inflammation. Leukocoria is not managed as an infection.

Imaging may be used in the workup, but a plain orbital x-ray is not the appropriate next step. The child needs urgent specialist evaluation with ophthalmic examination and appropriate imaging, typically including ocular ultrasound and MRI when indicated.
A white pupillary reflex is not a normal variant. Leukocoria is a red-flag finding that can indicate retinoblastoma or other serious ocular pathology.
Waiting for routine screening would delay diagnosis of a potentially vision- and life-threatening condition. Suspected retinoblastoma warrants urgent action now.

questions.teaching_point: Leukocoria in an infant is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise and requires urgent ophthalmology referral.

questions.vignette: A 61-year-old woman presents to her primary care clinic with 4 months of progressive bloating, early satiety, and intermittent pelvic pressure. She reports needing to urinate more often but denies dysuria or hematuria. She has also noticed that her clothes fit more tightly despite no major change in diet. She is postmenopausal and has no history of hormone use. Pelvic examination shows mild fullness in the left adnexa without tenderness. Her abdominal exam is otherwise benign. A urine pregnancy test is negative.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Endometriosis
Irritable bowel syndrome
Benign ovarian cyst
Urinary tract infection
Ovarian cancer

questions.rationale: Ovarian cancer is the most likely diagnosis. In a postmenopausal woman, several months of persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pressure, and urinary frequency are concerning for an ovarian malignancy, especially when pelvic examination reveals adnexal fullness. Ovarian cancer often presents with vague gastrointestinal and urinary symptoms and is commonly diagnosed late because the presentation can mimic benign disorders.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Endometriosis may cause pelvic pain and adnexal findings, but it usually begins earlier in reproductive life and is less likely to present for the first time after menopause with this pattern of symptoms.
Irritable bowel syndrome can cause bloating, but it would not explain adnexal fullness on examination or the postmenopausal onset of persistent early satiety and pelvic pressure.
A benign ovarian cyst can cause adnexal fullness, but the prolonged, progressive symptoms in a postmenopausal patient—especially bloating and early satiety—are more concerning for malignancy.

A urinary tract infection can cause urinary frequency, but it would not typically cause months of progressive bloating, early satiety, or adnexal fullness, and the absence of dysuria makes it less likely.

questions.teaching_point: In postmenopausal patients, persistent bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency, and adnexal fullness should raise concern for ovarian cancer.

questions.vignette: A 78-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his daughter because of increasing confusion and a new inability to walk over the past 2 days. He has a 10-year history of Parkinson disease treated with carbidopa-levodopa. His daughter reports that he has been taking his medications inconsistently since developing nausea and poor appetite, and he has spent most of the last 2 days in bed. In the ED, he is afebrile, blood pressure is 148/84 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, and respiratory rate is 16/min. He is alert but slow to respond. He has marked rigidity, a resting tremor, and severe bradykinesia. There is no focal weakness. When asked to stand, he requires two people to assist and shuffles forward with very short steps. His mucous membranes are dry.
questions.lead_in: Which history or physical examination finding in this patient is the most concerning clue that his acute decline is due to worsening Parkinson symptoms rather than a new structural neurologic event?

answer_choices.text: The need for two-person assistance to stand and ambulate
The dry mucous membranes on examination
The resting tremor that is present during the examination
The marked increase in rigidity and bradykinesia after missed doses of carbidopa-levodopa
The mild slowing in his response to questions

questions.rationale: Missed doses of carbidopa-levodopa followed by worsening rigidity, bradykinesia, and gait dysfunction strongly support an acute exacerbation of Parkinson disease symptoms from dopaminergic withdrawal or undertreatment. In a patient with known Parkinson disease, this pattern is a key historical clue that the decline is medication-related rather than caused by a new focal structural lesion such as stroke, especially because the exam lacks focal weakness or other lateralizing findings.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Severe gait impairment is concerning, but without the medication history it is less specific. In Parkinson disease, loss of ambulation can occur during medication interruption and does not by itself distinguish this from another acute neurologic process.

Dry mucous membranes suggest dehydration, which may contribute to weakness or delirium, but they are nonspecific and do not specifically point to Parkinson symptom worsening over a structural neurologic cause.

A resting tremor is a classic chronic feature of Parkinson disease, but by itself it does not explain the acute deterioration or help distinguish medication-related worsening from a new neurologic event.

Mild slowed responses may reflect baseline Parkinson-related bradyphrenia, medication effects, or delirium; it is nonspecific and does not identify the key clue that the decline followed missed dopaminergic therapy.

questions.teaching_point: In known Parkinson disease, an acute worsening of rigidity, bradykinesia, and gait after missed levodopa doses is a major clue to medication-related decompensation rather than a new focal neurologic lesion.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man comes to a primary care clinic because of a headache that started 2 days ago and has steadily worsened. He reports mild nausea and feels "off balance" when walking. Three weeks ago he slipped on ice and struck the left side of his head, but he did not lose consciousness and did not seek care because he felt fine afterward. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. His blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg, pulse is 76/min, and he is afebrile. He is alert and oriented. Neurologic examination shows slight right pronator drift, slowed rapid alternating movements in the right hand, and a mildly unsteady gait. Pupils are equal and reactive, and there is no neck stiffness.
questions.lead_in: Which historical finding in this patient is the strongest clue that his symptoms are due to an intracranial hemorrhage rather than a primary headache disorder?

answer_choices.text: He is able to remain alert and oriented
He has a family history of migraine headaches
He has mild nausea with the headache
His blood pressure is mildly elevated at the clinic visit
The headache began several days after a minor head injury

questions.rationale: A delayed, progressively worsening headache after even minor head trauma is a classic historical clue for intracranial hemorrhage, especially a subdural hematoma. The risk is further increased by warfarin use, and the focal neurologic findings support an intracranial process rather than a primary headache disorder.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Being alert and oriented does not exclude intracranial hemorrhage; many patients with subdural hematoma remain awake and have subtle focal findings early on.
A family history of migraine may support a primary headache disorder, but it does not explain the delayed onset after head trauma or the focal neurologic deficits.
Nausea can occur with many headache syndromes, including migraine and intracranial hemorrhage, so it is not the strongest clue here.
Mildly elevated blood pressure is common during pain or stress and is not a specific clue to intracranial hemorrhage in this presentation.

questions.teaching_point: In an outpatient patient with headache after recent head trauma, especially on anticoagulation, a delayed worsening course and focal deficits should raise concern for intracranial hemorrhage.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man is admitted for worsening fatigue, diffuse back pain, and decreased appetite over 3 months. He also reports intermittent constipation and has had two recent falls. Vital signs are normal. Exam shows pallor and midline tenderness over the lower thoracic spine. Laboratory studies reveal hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), calcium 11.4 mg/dL, and total protein 9.8 g/dL with albumin 2.7 g/dL. Urinalysis is negative for blood and infection. Plain lumbar spine radiographs show no acute fracture.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the best next step to evaluate the suspected underlying disorder causing this patient's anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, and bone pain?

answer_choices.text: Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast
Urine calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio
Serum parathyroid hormone level
Thoracic spine magnetic resonance imaging
Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light chain assay, and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation

questions.rationale: This patient has findings strongly suggestive of multiple myeloma, including anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, bone pain, and elevated total protein with a low albumin level, which implies a large globulin gap. The best next diagnostic step is to look for monoclonal protein with serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation, serum free light chain assay, and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation. These studies are the appropriate initial laboratory evaluation for suspected plasma cell dyscrasia; bone marrow biopsy is used after monoclonal protein testing supports the diagnosis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis may help evaluate metastatic malignancy or other structural disease, but it does not directly assess for monoclonal protein and is not the best initial study when multiple myeloma is suspected.

A urine calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio is used to help distinguish familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia from primary hyperparathyroidism and does not evaluate a suspected plasma cell dyscrasia.

A parathyroid hormone level is useful in the evaluation of hypercalcemia, but this patient's anemia, renal dysfunction, bone pain, and marked protein gap make multiple myeloma the more likely underlying disorder to evaluate first.
Thoracic spine MRI can identify focal marrow lesions or occult vertebral compression fractures, but it is not the best first diagnostic study for confirming suspected multiple myeloma.

questions.teaching_point: When multiple myeloma is suspected, initial evaluation should include serum and urine testing for monoclonal protein, along with serum free light chains; bone marrow biopsy follows to confirm the diagnosis.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old man is admitted after falling from a ladder and landing on his right foot. He has significant midfoot pain and swelling and is unable to bear weight. Examination shows tenderness over the dorsal midfoot with pain worsened by forefoot abduction; skin is intact and distal pulses are present. Plain radiographs of the foot show a nondisplaced navicular fracture. Orthopedics is consulted.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Perform immediate operative fixation in the operating room
Immobilize the foot and ankle in a short-leg splint or cast, keep the patient non–weight-bearing, and arrange urgent orthopedic follow-up
Place the patient in a walking boot and allow weight bearing as tolerated
Begin range-of-motion exercises and advance activity as tolerated
Discharge the patient with crutches and simple analgesics only

questions.rationale: A nondisplaced navicular fracture should be protected with immobilization and strict non–weight-bearing because the navicular has a tenuous blood supply and is important for midfoot stability. In the acute setting, a short-leg splint or cast is appropriate initial management while orthopedic follow-up is arranged. Definitive management depends on fracture pattern and clinical course, but immediate weight bearing or unprotected discharge is inappropriate.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Immediate operative fixation is not routine for a nondisplaced navicular fracture; surgery is generally reserved for displaced, unstable, comminuted, or irreducible injuries.
A walking boot with weight bearing as tolerated is too permissive for an acute navicular fracture and risks displacement or delayed union.
Early range-of-motion and activity advancement are inappropriate for an acute navicular fracture because the bone must be immobilized to heal properly.
Crutches and analgesics alone do not adequately immobilize the fracture or protect the navicular from weight-bearing stress.

questions.teaching_point: Initial management of a nondisplaced navicular fracture is immobilization with non–weight-bearing status and urgent orthopedic follow-up to protect a bone with limited blood supply.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is admitted after several recent falls. His wife reports that over the past year he has become slower with dressing and rising from a chair, and his handwriting has become progressively smaller. On exam, he has a masked facies, a resting tremor in his right hand that lessens when he reaches for a cup, and a shuffling gait with reduced arm swing. Strength is full, reflexes are normal, and sensation is intact.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding would most strongly support the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Hyperreflexia with ankle clonus and spastic gait
Proximal muscle weakness with a positive Gowers maneuver
Wide-based gait with loss of vibration sense in the feet
Intention tremor that worsens as he reaches for a target
Cogwheel rigidity with increased resistance during passive movement

questions.rationale: Parkinson disease is characterized by bradykinesia plus resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability. Cogwheel rigidity on passive range of motion is a classic exam finding that, along with the patient’s masked facies, shuffling gait, reduced arm swing, and resting tremor, supports the diagnosis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Hyperreflexia, clonus, and spastic gait suggest an upper motor neuron syndrome such as cervical myelopathy or stroke, not Parkinson disease.
Proximal weakness with a Gowers maneuver points to a myopathic process such as polymyositis or muscular dystrophy rather than a basal ganglia disorder.
A wide-based gait with impaired vibration sense suggests sensory ataxia from peripheral neuropathy or posterior column dysfunction, which is different from the shuffling gait of Parkinson disease.
An intention tremor that worsens with goal-directed movement is more consistent with cerebellar dysfunction, not the resting tremor typical of Parkinson disease.

questions.teaching_point: Parkinson disease is suggested by bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability; cogwheel rigidity is a key physical exam finding.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man comes to the emergency department 1 day after an open upper abdominal surgery for bowel obstruction. He reports increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough since this morning. He has been reluctant to take deep breaths because of incisional pain. He is afebrile, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg, pulse is 104/min, respiratory rate is 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. On examination, the chest expansion is slightly decreased at the right base, and breath sounds are diminished over the right lower lung field with faint end-inspiratory crackles. There is no leg swelling, wheezing, or pleuritic chest pain.
questions.lead_in: Which physical examination finding is most consistent with this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Diffuse expiratory wheezing with prolonged expiratory phase
Egophony and bronchial breath sounds over a focal lung segment
Unilateral hyperresonance to percussion with absent breath sounds
Prominent jugular venous distention with bilateral lower-extremity edema
Decreased tactile fremitus with dullness to percussion over the affected area

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has postoperative atelectasis from shallow breathing due to pain after abdominal surgery. Atelectasis commonly causes reduced chest expansion, diminished breath sounds, decreased tactile fremitus, and dullness to percussion over the affected region. Mild hypoxemia and tachypnea are also common in the early postoperative setting.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Diffuse expiratory wheezing and a prolonged expiratory phase suggest an obstructive process such as asthma or COPD exacerbation rather than localized postoperative volume loss.
Egophony and bronchial breath sounds are classic for lung consolidation, such as pneumonia, which would be more likely to produce fever, productive cough, or a more focal infectious picture.

Unilateral hyperresonance with absent breath sounds is more consistent with pneumothorax, which would usually present more abruptly and often with pleuritic chest pain or significant respiratory distress.
Jugular venous distention and bilateral edema suggest volume overload or heart failure, not a localized postoperative pulmonary process causing unilateral decreased aeration.

questions.teaching_point: Postoperative atelectasis typically presents with shallow breathing, diminished breath sounds, decreased fremitus, and dullness to percussion in the affected lung base.

questions.vignette: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of sudden, intermittent episodes of severe crying and drawing his legs up to his abdomen that began earlier today. Between episodes, he becomes unusually quiet and drowsy. His mother reports two episodes of nonbilious vomiting and one stool mixed with mucus and dark red blood. He had a mild upper respiratory infection last week but has otherwise been healthy. On examination, he is afebrile, intermittently irritable, and mildly dehydrated. His abdomen is soft but mildly distended.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical finding would most strongly support the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Diffuse abdominal rigidity with absent bowel sounds and fever
Tenderness and guarding localized to the right lower quadrant with rebound pain
Projective nonbilious vomiting with an olive-like mass palpated in the epigastrium
A tender, nonreducible bulge in the groin that becomes more prominent with crying
A palpable, elongated abdominal mass, often in the right upper quadrant, that may be difficult to distinguish from surrounding bowel

questions.rationale: This infant has classic intussusception: intermittent colicky abdominal pain, lethargy between episodes, vomiting, and bloody mucus stool. A supportive physical finding is a palpable sausage-shaped or elongated abdominal mass, often in the right upper quadrant, caused by telescoping of one segment of bowel into another. This finding strongly supports intussusception in the appropriate clinical context.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Diffuse rigidity, fever, and absent bowel sounds suggest advanced peritonitis or perforation, which is a complication or alternate diagnosis rather than a typical supporting finding for intussusception.
Right lower quadrant rebound and guarding suggest appendicitis or generalized peritoneal irritation rather than the intermittent obstructive symptoms and bloody stool seen with intussusception.
Projective nonbilious vomiting with an olive-like epigastric mass is characteristic of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which typically presents in younger infants and does not cause bloody stools.
A tender, nonreducible groin bulge suggests an incarcerated inguinal hernia, which can cause obstruction but does not match the classic episodic pain, lethargy, and currant-jelly stool pattern.

questions.teaching_point: Intussusception in infants typically causes intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, lethargy, and bloody mucus stools; a sausage-shaped abdominal mass is a classic supportive examination finding.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of worsening weakness, nausea, diffuse abdominal pain, and lightheadedness. She reports a 6-month history of unintentional weight loss, salt craving, and increasing fatigue. She has vitiligo and takes no regular medications. Today she appears ill and anxious. Blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, and temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F). Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and generalized hyperpigmentation, including darkening of the palmar creases and gums. Laboratory studies are notable for sodium 124 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L, glucose 62 mg/dL, and bicarbonate 18 mEq/L.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Secondary adrenal insufficiency
Hemochromatosis
Primary adrenal insufficiency
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Chronic kidney disease with uremia

questions.rationale: Primary adrenal insufficiency is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has chronic constitutional symptoms, salt craving, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and hyperpigmentation. The hyperpigmentation occurs because loss of adrenal cortisol leads to increased ACTH production, and ACTH stimulates melanocytes. Autoimmune adrenal destruction is supported by the associated vitiligo.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Secondary adrenal insufficiency can cause fatigue, hypotension, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia, but aldosterone secretion is usually preserved, so hyperkalemia and salt craving are less likely. Hyperpigmentation is also absent because ACTH is low.
Hemochromatosis can cause fatigue and skin hyperpigmentation, but it does not typically cause hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, salt craving, or acute adrenal crisis physiology with severe hypotension.

Diabetic ketoacidosis can present with abdominal pain, dehydration, hypotension, and metabolic acidosis, but it usually causes marked hyperglycemia rather than hypoglycemia and does not explain chronic hyperpigmentation or salt craving.
Chronic kidney disease can cause fatigue, nausea, and hyperkalemia, but it would not typically cause salt craving, hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, or a syndrome of progressive adrenal failure.

questions.teaching_point: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and hyperpigmentation due to elevated ACTH from adrenal failure.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of worsening fever and right ear pain for 5 days. He was seen at an urgent care clinic 2 weeks ago for acute otitis media and completed amoxicillin, but his symptoms never fully resolved. Over the past day, his parents noticed increasing swelling and redness behind the right ear and that the ear seems pushed outward. On examination, he is febrile and irritable. The right mastoid area is tender, erythematous, and swollen. Otoscopic examination shows a bulging, opaque tympanic membrane on the right.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Otitis externa
Peritonsillar abscess
Auricular perichondritis
Acute bacterial sinusitis
Mastoiditis

questions.rationale: This child has classic acute mastoiditis complicating acute otitis media: persistent or worsening ear infection symptoms followed by postauricular erythema, swelling, mastoid tenderness, and auricular protrusion. The bulging, opaque tympanic membrane supports ongoing middle ear infection. Mastoiditis is a clinical diagnosis suggested by these exam findings.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Otitis externa usually presents with ear canal pain, tragal tenderness, and canal edema or discharge rather than postauricular swelling after recent otitis media.
Peritonsillar abscess typically causes severe sore throat, muffled voice, trismus, and uvular deviation, not postauricular swelling or ear displacement.

Auricular perichondritis affects the pinna, often after trauma or piercing, and causes auricular erythema and swelling while typically sparing the ear lobe; it does not cause mastoid tenderness or a bulging tympanic membrane.
Acute bacterial sinusitis can cause fever, nasal discharge, and facial pressure, but it does not cause mastoid tenderness or outward displacement of the ear.

questions.teaching_point: Mastoiditis is a complication of acute otitis media characterized by postauricular swelling, erythema, mastoid tenderness, and auricular protrusion.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD and chronic home oxygen use is admitted for pneumonia. Two days later, he suddenly develops worsening dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain while walking to the bathroom. He is tachypneic, speaking in short phrases, and using accessory muscles. Blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg, heart rate is 124/min, respiratory rate is 32/min, and oxygen saturation is 84% on his usual 2 L/min nasal cannula. On exam, the right hemithorax has markedly decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance. Chest radiograph confirms a large right pneumothorax with mediastinal shift.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

answer_choices.text: Immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube placement
Obtain emergent CT angiography of the chest to evaluate for pulmonary embolism
Administer high-flow oxygen and repeat chest radiography in 6 hours
Perform emergent chest tube placement without prior needle decompression
Start intravenous furosemide for presumed acute decompensated heart failure

questions.rationale: This patient has a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax with tension physiology, evidenced by acute respiratory distress, hypotension, unilateral decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance, and mediastinal shift. In an unstable patient, the immediate intervention is needle decompression to rapidly relieve intrapleural pressure, followed by definitive chest tube placement. Treatment should not be delayed for additional imaging or observation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pulmonary embolism can cause acute dyspnea and hypoxemia, but the unilateral exam findings and radiographic mediastinal shift indicate tension pneumothorax, which requires immediate bedside decompression rather than CT imaging.
High-flow oxygen and observation may be appropriate for a small, stable pneumothorax, but this patient is unstable with tension physiology and requires emergent decompression.
Chest tube placement is definitive therapy for pneumothorax, but in a patient with tension physiology, immediate needle decompression is performed first to rapidly relieve pleural pressure.
Furosemide would treat volume overload or cardiogenic pulmonary edema, not a tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic compromise.

questions.teaching_point: A secondary pneumothorax with instability or tension physiology requires immediate needle decompression, then chest tube placement; do not delay treatment for additional imaging.

questions.vignette: A 10-year-old boy is brought to clinic 2 days after being hit in the head by a baseball during practice. He did not lose consciousness and was observed in the emergency department for several hours without acute findings. Since then, he has had intermittent headache, difficulty concentrating at school, and nausea after reading for long periods. He has not vomited, has no focal weakness, and his neurologic examination is normal. His mother asks when he can return to sports because he feels "mostly fine."
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Order an urgent head CT scan to rule out a delayed epidural hematoma
Provide a graduated return-to-learn and return-to-play plan with close follow-up
Start acetaminophen-codeine for postconcussive headache and clear him for practice once symptoms improve
Refer for immediate neurosurgical evaluation for suspected intracranial hemorrhage
Recommend strict bed rest in a dark room until all symptoms resolve completely

questions.rationale: This child has a mild traumatic brain injury/concussion with persistent but improving symptoms, normal neurologic exam, and no red flags for an emergent intracranial process. Management is outpatient with cognitive and physical rest for the first 24–48 hours followed by a gradual, symptom-limited return-to-learn and return-to-play protocol, with follow-up to monitor recovery. Premature return to contact sports increases the risk of prolonged symptoms and repeat injury.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Urgent CT is not indicated in a neurologically normal child with a typical concussion course and no concerning features such as worsening headache, repeated vomiting, altered mental status, focal deficits, or signs of skull fracture.
Opioid-containing analgesics are not recommended for routine concussion symptoms, and symptom improvement alone does not justify immediate clearance for sports; a graded return protocol is needed.
There is no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage requiring emergent neurosurgical evaluation because the child is stable, neurologically intact, and lacks red-flag findings.
Prolonged strict bed rest is no longer recommended; brief relative rest is followed by gradual return to normal cognitive and physical activity as tolerated.

questions.teaching_point: After pediatric concussion, use brief relative rest, then a gradual return-to-learn/return-to-play plan rather than prolonged rest, immediate imaging, or early sports clearance.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 14-month-old boy is brought to clinic because his parents have noticed that his left eye sometimes appears white in flash photographs over the past 2 weeks. They also report that he has been bumping into furniture more often and seems to favor his right eye when reaching for toys. He was born at term and has no history of eye trauma or infection. On examination, the left pupil has an abnormal white reflex; the cornea is clear and there is no conjunctival injection or eye pain. The right eye examination is normal.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Arrange urgent referral to a pediatric ophthalmologist for dilated funduscopic examination under anesthesia
Reassure the parents that this finding is likely due to normal light reflection
Start topical erythromycin ointment and reassess in 1 week
Prescribe cyclopentolate drops and schedule follow-up in 2 weeks
Order orbital ultrasound and wait for results before referral

questions.rationale: An abnormal white pupillary reflex in a young child is concerning for retinoblastoma and requires urgent specialist evaluation. Dilated funduscopic examination by a pediatric ophthalmologist is the appropriate next step because prompt diagnosis is critical to preserve vision and assess for an intraocular tumor. Delay for empiric treatment or watchful waiting is inappropriate.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A white pupillary reflex is not a normal variant in this context and is a classic warning sign for serious ocular pathology that requires immediate evaluation.
Topical antibiotics are used for superficial bacterial eye infections, which would cause conjunctival redness or discharge rather than a persistent white pupillary reflex and visual behavior changes.
Cyclopentolate is used for uveitis or refraction-related issues, neither of which explains an abnormal white reflex and unilateral visual preference in a toddler.

Imaging may be part of the workup, but the priority is urgent ophthalmologic referral for definitive examination; waiting for imaging risks delaying diagnosis of a potentially vision- and life-threatening malignancy.

questions.teaching_point: A leukocoria in a child is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise and needs urgent pediatric ophthalmology referral.

questions.vignette: A 2-day-old term newborn is noted to become dusky when crying and improves only partially with supplemental oxygen. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. On exam, the infant has central cyanosis, a single loud second heart sound, and a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. The precordium is quiet, and the liver edge is not enlarged. Pulse oximetry remains in the low 80s despite oxygen therapy. A chest radiograph shows a normal-to-small cardiac silhouette with decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Tricuspid atresia
Patent ductus arteriosus
Tetralogy of Fallot
Transposition of the great arteries
Ventricular septal defect

questions.rationale: Tricuspid atresia causes cyanosis in the newborn because blood cannot pass normally from the right atrium to the right ventricle, so pulmonary blood flow depends on an associated shunt. Clues here include early neonatal cyanosis with poor response to oxygen, a single second heart sound, a quiet precordium, and decreased pulmonary vascular markings on chest radiograph, which fit a cyanotic congenital heart defect with reduced pulmonary blood flow.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus is usually acyanotic early on and is associated with bounding pulses and increased pulmonary blood flow; it does not explain persistent neonatal cyanosis with decreased pulmonary vascular markings.

Tetralogy of Fallot can cause cyanosis and decreased pulmonary vascular markings, but it usually presents with a harsh systolic ejection murmur from right ventricular outflow obstruction and is classically associated with hypercyanotic spells rather than a single loud S2.

Transposition of the great arteries also causes early cyanosis with poor oxygen response, but it more often has a normal chest radiograph with increased pulmonary blood flow or a narrow mediastinum rather than decreased pulmonary vascular markings and a quiet precordium.

A ventricular septal defect typically produces a left-to-right shunt and a holosystolic murmur after pulmonary vascular resistance falls; isolated VSD does not usually cause immediate cyanosis in the first days of life.

questions.teaching_point: In a cyanotic newborn with a single S2, quiet precordium, and decreased pulmonary blood flow on chest x-ray, think tricuspid atresia.

questions.vignette: A 15-year-old boy is brought to an outpatient endocrine visit because of several months of fatigue, constipation, and intermittent abdominal pain. His mother also reports that he has been drinking more water than usual and has had two kidney stones over the past year. Exam shows mild dehydration but is otherwise normal. Laboratory testing shows repeated mild hypercalcemia with an elevated intact parathyroid hormone level. Neck ultrasound suggests a single parathyroid adenoma.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive treatment for this patient?

answer_choices.text: Cinacalcet therapy
Parathyroidectomy
Loop diuretic therapy
Oral calcitriol supplementation
Observation with annual calcium monitoring

questions.rationale: Primary hyperparathyroidism in a child or adolescent with symptomatic hypercalcemia and complications such as nephrolithiasis is treated definitively with surgical removal of the overactive parathyroid tissue. Parathyroidectomy is the standard curative therapy when a parathyroid adenoma is identified.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cinacalcet can lower calcium in selected patients who are not surgical candidates, but it is not the preferred definitive treatment for a symptomatic adolescent with a parathyroid adenoma.
Loop diuretics may increase urinary calcium excretion in acute hypercalcemia management after hydration, but they do not address the underlying cause and are not definitive treatment.
Calcitriol would increase calcium levels and is used for hypocalcemia or vitamin D deficiency, not for primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia.
Observation is reserved for selected asymptomatic patients who do not meet criteria for surgery; this patient is symptomatic and has kidney stone complications, so monitoring alone is inappropriate.

questions.teaching_point: Symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, especially with nephrolithiasis, is definitively treated with parathyroidectomy.

questions.vignette: A 71-year-old man is brought to an outpatient clinic by his daughter because of 2 days of worsening headache, increasing confusion, and unsteady gait. Three weeks ago he fell backward off a step stool and struck the back of his head. He did not lose consciousness and did not seek care. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and lives alone.
