questions.teaching_point: Resistant hypertension with unexplained hypokalemia should be screened for primary aldosteronism using the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, with attention to factors such as diuretic use that can affect interpretation.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He receives dialysis on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and today is Thursday afternoon. His pre-op evaluation notes a left forearm arteriovenous fistula with a palpable thrill. Vital signs are stable, and he feels well. The surgical team asks which perioperative step is most appropriate to reduce the risk of dialysis access complications.
questions.lead_in: Which perioperative action is most appropriate for this patient?

answer_choices.text: Apply a pressure tourniquet over the fistula arm to improve venous return during surgery
Request that the fistula be clamped before transport to the operating room
Place an arterial line in the fistula arm because the access provides reliable arterial monitoring
Avoid blood pressure measurements and IV placement in the arm with the arteriovenous fistula
Place a routine peripheral IV in the fistula arm because it provides the best venous access

questions.rationale: Patients with a functioning arteriovenous fistula should have that extremity protected perioperatively to preserve access patency and avoid thrombosis, infiltration, hematoma, or stenosis. Blood pressure cuffs, venipuncture, peripheral IVs, and arterial lines should be avoided in the fistula arm whenever possible.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A tourniquet can obstruct venous outflow and damage the access, increasing the risk of thrombosis and loss of fistula function.
Clamping a functioning arteriovenous fistula can interrupt blood flow and threaten access patency. It is not a routine perioperative precaution.
An arterial line should not be placed in the fistula arm because arterial cannulation can compromise fistula flow or cause access injury.
Using the fistula arm for a routine peripheral IV can injure the access and increase the risk of infiltration, venous damage, or thrombosis.

questions.teaching_point: In patients with hemodialysis access, protect the fistula arm by avoiding blood pressure cuffs, IVs, venipuncture, and arterial cannulation to preserve long-term access function.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old woman comes for a wellness visit. Her father had medullary thyroid carcinoma in his early 40s, and her older brother was treated for an adrenal tumor after episodic headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. Genetic testing in the family identified a pathogenic RET mutation, and the patient has not yet been tested. She feels well today and takes no medications. Her blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg, and examination of the neck is unremarkable. She asks what preventive care is most appropriate for her now.
questions.lead_in: Which preventive recommendation is the most appropriate next step for this patient?

answer_choices.text: Refer her for RET genetic counseling and testing, with counseling about MEN 2A-associated surveillance if positive
Begin yearly thyroid ultrasound screening because physical examination is normal
Recommend no additional testing unless she develops symptoms of endocrine disease
Order annual plasma metanephrines starting at age 40 unless symptoms develop sooner
Obtain a serum calcitonin level now and repeat it annually if normal

questions.rationale: This patient has a strong family history of MEN 2A and a known pathogenic RET mutation in her family, so the most appropriate preventive step is genetic counseling and RET testing. If she is found to carry the mutation, she would then need syndrome-specific surveillance and risk-reducing management, including evaluation for medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism. Because MEN 2A is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance, asymptomatic adults with an affected first-degree relative should not wait for symptoms before evaluation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Thyroid ultrasound may detect nodules, but it is not the recommended screening strategy for a person at high genetic risk for MEN 2A. A normal neck exam does not rule out early medullary thyroid carcinoma, and definitive preventive planning should begin with RET counseling and testing.

Doing nothing until symptoms appear would miss the opportunity for early identification of a hereditary cancer syndrome. MEN 2A requires proactive family-based risk assessment and genetic evaluation even in asymptomatic adults.

Pheochromocytoma screening is important in MEN 2A, but starting annual plasma metanephrines at age 40 is too late and not the most appropriate first step here. Her immediate preventive priority is RET testing and counseling; surveillance timing would depend on mutation status and guideline-based family risk assessment.

Serum calcitonin can be used in the evaluation or follow-up of medullary thyroid carcinoma, but it is not the best initial preventive step in someone with a known familial RET mutation. Genetic counseling and RET testing come first because they determine the need for targeted surveillance and prophylactic management.

questions.teaching_point: In an asymptomatic adult with a first-degree relative who has a known RET mutation, the next preventive step is genetic counseling and RET testing, not symptom-based watchful waiting.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 29-year-old man is evaluated in the preoperative clinic 2 days after being struck in the left eye by a baseball. He has persistent diplopia when looking upward, left periorbital swelling, and numbness over the left cheek. Visual acuity is unchanged, pupils are equal and reactive, and there is no hyphema. On exam, upward gaze is limited in the injured eye and there is palpable step-off along the orbital floor. The surgeon is concerned about an orbital floor fracture with possible entrapment before operative repair is planned.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to further evaluate this injury before surgery?

answer_choices.text: Ultrasound of the globe
MRI of the orbits with contrast
Plain radiographs of the facial bones
Noncontrast CT scan of the orbits and facial bones
Fluorescein staining with slit-lamp examination

questions.rationale: Noncontrast CT of the orbits and facial bones is the best study for suspected blowout fracture because it clearly identifies orbital floor defects, herniation of orbital contents, and extraocular muscle entrapment. It is the preferred imaging test for defining the extent of injury and helping guide operative planning.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Ultrasound may be used in select ocular conditions, but it is not the preferred test for suspected orbital floor fracture and does not adequately define bony defects for surgical planning.

MRI is not the initial study for acute orbital trauma because it is slower, less available, and less useful than CT for evaluating bony injury. It is also not ideal when urgent preoperative assessment is needed.
Plain radiographs can miss orbital floor fractures and provide limited detail about soft tissue herniation or muscle entrapment, making them inferior to CT in this setting.
Fluorescein staining with slit-lamp examination helps evaluate corneal abrasion or epithelial defects, but it does not assess the bony orbit or extraocular muscle entrapment.

questions.teaching_point: Noncontrast CT of the orbits is the imaging study of choice for suspected blowout fracture because it best shows orbital floor disruption and soft tissue entrapment.

questions.vignette: A 46-year-old woman comes to clinic because of intermittent tingling around her mouth and in both hands for the past week. She also reports painful muscle cramping in her feet, especially when driving or writing for long periods. She had a thyroidectomy 2 months ago and is taking no calcium supplements. Vital signs are normal. On examination, tapping over the facial nerve in front of the ear causes twitching of the ipsilateral facial muscles. Strength is otherwise normal, and the remainder of the neurologic examination is unremarkable.
questions.lead_in: Which physical examination finding is most consistent with this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Carpopedal spasm elicited by inflating a blood pressure cuff
Flaccid proximal muscle weakness that improves with repeated effort
Hyperreflexia with ankle clonus after voluntary muscle contraction
Resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity
Ptosis that worsens with sustained upward gaze

questions.rationale: This patient likely has hypocalcemia due to postoperative hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy. Her perioral tingling and painful muscle cramping are classic symptoms of neuromuscular irritability caused by low calcium. A blood pressure cuff inflated on the arm can provoke carpopedal spasm, known as Trousseau sign, which is a classic physical finding of hypocalcemia.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Flaccid proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort suggests a fatigable neuromuscular junction disorder such as myasthenia gravis, not hypocalcemia.
Hyperreflexia with ankle clonus can occur with neuromuscular irritability or upper motor neuron disorders, but it is not the classic physical finding used to identify hypocalcemia in this setting.
Resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity is characteristic of Parkinson disease and does not match postoperative hypocalcemia.
Ptosis that worsens with sustained upward gaze is a classic sign of myasthenia gravis, not the tetany and paresthesias caused by hypocalcemia.

questions.teaching_point: Hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy can cause perioral paresthesias, muscle cramps, and tetany; Trousseau sign is carpopedal spasm induced by blood pressure cuff inflation.

questions.vignette: A 48-year-old woman comes to clinic for follow-up of persistent hypertension despite taking amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. She reports intermittent muscle cramps and fatigue. Her blood pressure is 162/96 mm Hg, and repeat measurements over the past 2 visits have been similarly elevated. Basic metabolic panel shows potassium 3.1 mEq/L and bicarbonate 31 mEq/L. She denies vomiting, diarrhea, licorice use, or use of over-the-counter decongestants. Her kidney function is normal.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to evaluate this patient’s likely underlying condition?

answer_choices.text: Plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity to calculate the aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Serum catecholamines and metanephrines
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
Renal artery duplex ultrasonography
24-hour urinary free cortisol measurement

questions.rationale: This patient has persistent hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, which strongly suggests primary aldosteronism. The best initial diagnostic study is measurement of plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity to calculate the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, which is the recommended screening test before confirmatory testing and adrenal imaging. Because some antihypertensives can influence renin and aldosterone levels, medication effects should be considered when preparing for testing, but the aldosterone-to-renin ratio remains the correct next step.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Serum catecholamines and metanephrines are used to assess pheochromocytoma, which typically causes episodic headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, and labile blood pressure rather than this pattern of persistent hypertension with hypokalemia.
CT imaging can help localize an adrenal lesion after biochemical evidence of primary aldosteronism, but it is not the initial diagnostic study.

Renal artery duplex ultrasonography evaluates for renovascular hypertension, but the electrolyte pattern here is more consistent with primary aldosteronism, so aldosterone-renin testing should come first.
24-hour urinary free cortisol is used to evaluate hypercortisolism, which can cause hypertension but does not best explain the combination of hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis here.

questions.teaching_point: In adults with persistent hypertension plus hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, the first diagnostic step is screening for primary aldosteronism with an aldosterone-to-renin ratio, not immediate adrenal imaging.

questions.vignette: A 28-year-old man is seen in the clinic 2 days after falling off a bicycle and striking his head on pavement while wearing no helmet. He did not lose consciousness but had brief confusion for several minutes. Since the injury, he has had headache, difficulty concentrating at work, and increased fatigue. He denies vomiting, seizure, worsening headache, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, focal weakness, or worsening neck pain. Neurologic examination is normal, and his vital signs are stable.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

answer_choices.text: Refer for immediate neurosurgical evaluation
Provide concussion education and advise 24 to 48 hours of relative physical and cognitive rest followed by gradual return to activity as tolerated
Start prophylactic levetiracetam to prevent posttraumatic seizures
Prescribe a 10-day course of dexamethasone to reduce cerebral edema
Order an urgent noncontrast head CT scan

questions.rationale: This patient has an uncomplicated mild traumatic brain injury (concussion). He is neurologically intact, has no anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and has no red-flag symptoms such as vomiting, worsening headache, seizure, focal deficits, or signs of skull fracture. The appropriate outpatient management is concussion education, brief relative rest for 24 to 48 hours, symptom monitoring, and a gradual return to normal activity as tolerated. Emergent imaging or specialty referral is not routinely indicated in this scenario.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Immediate neurosurgical evaluation is not needed for a mild head injury with a normal neurologic examination and no evidence of intracranial complication.
Routine antiseizure prophylaxis is not indicated for an uncomplicated concussion without intracranial hemorrhage or severe traumatic brain injury.
Corticosteroids are not recommended for routine management of traumatic brain injury or concussion and do not improve outcomes in this setting.

Urgent head CT is reserved for patients with concerning features such as worsening symptoms, focal neurologic deficits, repeated vomiting, seizure, skull fracture signs, anticoagulant use, or other high-risk findings. This patient has none of those features.

questions.teaching_point: Uncomplicated concussion after mild traumatic brain injury is managed as an outpatient with education, brief relative rest, and a gradual return to activity unless red-flag symptoms suggest the need for urgent imaging or escalation of care.

questions.vignette: A 32-year-old man is seen in a family medicine clinic 2 days after striking the right side of his head on a cabinet door while standing up. He had no loss of consciousness and returned to work the next day, but since the injury he has had a constant headache, difficulty concentrating, and increased sensitivity to light. He denies vomiting, weakness, seizure, or worsening confusion. His vital signs are normal, and neurologic examination shows no focal deficits. He has not taken any anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents. He asks what he should do to recover as quickly as possible and avoid making symptoms worse.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management recommendation at this time?

answer_choices.text: Start high-dose corticosteroids to reduce cerebral edema and post-injury inflammation
Advise relative physical and cognitive rest for 24 to 48 hours followed by a gradual, symptom-limited return to activity
Recommend immediate return to full work and exercise to prevent prolonged postconcussive symptoms
Obtain an urgent noncontrast head CT scan and send him to the emergency department
Prescribe prophylactic levetiracetam to prevent a delayed post-traumatic seizure

questions.rationale: This patient has a mild traumatic brain injury/concussion without red-flag features such as loss of consciousness, progressive neurologic deficit, repeated vomiting, seizure, anticoagulant use, or altered mental status. Initial outpatient management is brief relative rest for 24 to 48 hours, then a gradual, symptom-limited return to normal cognitive and physical activities. Prolonged strict rest is not helpful, but immediate full activity can worsen symptoms and delay recovery.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Corticosteroids are not recommended for routine management of mild traumatic brain injury and have no proven benefit in this setting.
Immediate full return to activity can exacerbate postconcussive symptoms; recovery is better supported by a gradual return after a brief rest period.

Although imaging is needed if red-flag features are present, this presentation is consistent with uncomplicated concussion and does not require urgent ED referral or CT based on the information given.
Routine seizure prophylaxis is not indicated for uncomplicated mild TBI without intracranial hemorrhage, seizure, or severe injury.

questions.teaching_point: Uncomplicated concussion is managed with brief rest, then gradual symptom-limited return to activity; urgent imaging is reserved for red flags.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of new easy bruising and gum bleeding for 2 days. She had a viral upper respiratory infection last week and takes no prescription medications. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and pulse is 84/min. Exam shows scattered petechiae on the lower extremities and no hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or neurologic deficits. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 7,400/mm3, and platelet count 8,000/mm3. Peripheral smear shows isolated thrombocytopenia without platelet clumping or schistocytes. She has mucosal bleeding but no hemodynamic instability or evidence of intracranial or gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

answer_choices.text: Platelet transfusion
Desmopressin
Rituximab
Corticosteroids
Fresh frozen plasma

questions.rationale: This patient has immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), suggested by isolated severe thrombocytopenia, mucocutaneous bleeding, and a recent viral illness. In a stable patient with symptomatic ITP, the most appropriate initial treatment is a corticosteroid to reduce immune-mediated platelet destruction. Oral prednisone or dexamethasone are commonly used; IV corticosteroids can also be given in the emergency setting if parenteral treatment is desired. Platelet transfusion is not first-line because transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed unless there is life-threatening bleeding.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Platelet transfusion is generally reserved for life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedures in immune thrombocytopenia because transfused platelets may be rapidly destroyed.
Desmopressin is used to improve platelet adhesion in disorders such as von Willebrand disease or to help platelet dysfunction from uremia, not to treat immune-mediated platelet destruction.
Rituximab is a second-line therapy for immune thrombocytopenia and is not the usual initial treatment in the emergency department.
Fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors and is used for coagulopathy, not isolated thrombocytopenia due to immune thrombocytopenia.

questions.teaching_point: First-line treatment for symptomatic immune thrombocytopenia in a stable patient is corticosteroids; platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedures.

questions.vignette: A 38-year-old man is admitted for severe right-sided headaches that occur 2-3 times per day for the past week. Each attack starts suddenly, peaks within minutes, and lasts about 45 minutes. During attacks he is restless and paces the room. He has tearing of the right eye, nasal congestion, and a red eye on the same side. His neurologic exam is normal between attacks, and a head CT obtained in the emergency department is unrevealing. The current episode began 20 minutes ago and he is in visible distress despite taking oral ibuprofen earlier today. He has known coronary artery disease and reports that he was told not to use triptans.
questions.lead_in: Which treatment is the most appropriate next step to abort his current headache attack?

answer_choices.text: Oral propranolol
Oral prednisone
High-flow 100% oxygen via nonrebreather mask
Oral sumatriptan
Subcutaneous sumatriptan

questions.rationale: High-flow 100% oxygen delivered by nonrebreather mask is a first-line abortive treatment for an acute cluster headache attack and can relieve pain rapidly. In this patient, oxygen is the best next step because he has known coronary artery disease and should avoid triptans, including subcutaneous sumatriptan. Oral medications are generally too slow to abort a cluster headache attack effectively.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Propranolol is used for migraine prevention, not for aborting an acute cluster headache attack.
Oral prednisone may be used as transitional therapy to reduce cluster frequency during a bout, but it does not rapidly abort an active headache attack.
Oral sumatriptan can treat migraine but is too slow for a cluster headache attack and triptans should be avoided in this patient because of coronary artery disease.
Subcutaneous sumatriptan is an effective abortive therapy for cluster headache in appropriate patients, but it is contraindicated here because of the patient's coronary artery disease.

questions.teaching_point: Acute cluster headache attacks are aborted with high-flow oxygen or a rapid-acting triptan; when triptans are contraindicated, high-flow oxygen is an appropriate first-line abortive therapy.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old woman comes to the office for worsening right knee pain for the past 8 months. The pain is dull and worse after she walks long distances or climbs stairs. She has morning stiffness that lasts about 10 minutes and improves as she gets moving. She has no fever, redness, or swelling. She has hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. She has already tried weight loss, exercise, acetaminophen, and an over-the-counter knee brace without much relief. Exam shows crepitus and bony enlargement of the right knee with mild tenderness along the joint line and no effusion.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next medication to help manage her symptoms?

answer_choices.text: Topical diclofenac gel
Long-term oral prednisone
Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection
Duloxetine
Oral ibuprofen

questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, suggested by chronic activity-related pain, brief morning stiffness, crepitus, and bony enlargement without inflammatory signs. She has already tried appropriate nonpharmacologic measures and acetaminophen without adequate relief. A topical NSAID such as diclofenac gel is an appropriate next medication because it improves pain while limiting systemic exposure. This is especially helpful in a patient with stage 3 chronic kidney disease and hypertension, where oral NSAIDs should generally be avoided or used with great caution due to renal and blood pressure risks.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Long-term oral prednisone is not an appropriate treatment for osteoarthritis and exposes the patient to substantial systemic adverse effects without treating the underlying degenerative process.

Intra-articular hyaluronic acid has limited and variable benefit for knee osteoarthritis and is not preferred before topical NSAIDs; it is generally reserved for selected patients after simpler options fail.
Duloxetine can be used for chronic musculoskeletal pain, including osteoarthritis, but topical NSAID therapy is usually preferred first for localized knee symptoms when oral NSAIDs are undesirable.

Oral ibuprofen can relieve osteoarthritis pain, but it is a poor choice here because systemic NSAIDs can worsen kidney function and raise blood pressure in a patient with chronic kidney disease and hypertension.

questions.teaching_point: For symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, topical NSAIDs are a preferred treatment option after nonpharmacologic therapy and acetaminophen, especially when systemic NSAID toxicity is a concern such as in chronic kidney disease.

questions.vignette: A 15-year-old girl is brought to an outpatient pediatric visit by her mother for a sports physical. Over the past 4 months, she has lost 8 kg (18 lb). Her mother reports that she has cut out carbohydrates, avoids family meals, and exercises for an hour every day after school. The patient says she feels "fine" and is proud that she can fit into smaller clothes. She has not yet started menstruating. Vital signs show a heart rate of 52/min and blood pressure of 88/54 mm Hg. Body mass index is below the 5th percentile for age. She denies purging and substance use.
questions.lead_in: Which health maintenance recommendation is most appropriate at this visit?

answer_choices.text: Begin fluoxetine now to reduce restrictive eating behaviors and prevent further weight loss
Refer for psychotherapy alone because she denies purging and is still attending school regularly
Reassure the family that delayed menarche is likely due to athletics and advise watchful waiting without specific intervention

Recommend family-based treatment with nutritional rehabilitation, stop the excessive exercise, and arrange close medical follow-up with assessment for possible hospitalization if instability is confirmed
Continue outpatient sports participation while arranging routine dietary counseling and reassessing in several months

questions.rationale: This adolescent has anorexia nervosa with signs of medical compromise, including rapid weight loss, severe caloric restriction, excessive exercise, low body mass index, primary amenorrhea/delayed pubertal development, bradycardia, and hypotension. The most appropriate management is a multidisciplinary approach centered on nutritional rehabilitation, family-based treatment when feasible, and restriction of excessive exercise. Because her vital signs suggest possible medical instability, she also needs prompt assessment for hospitalization or a higher level of care depending on orthostatic vitals, temperature, electrolytes, ECG findings, and degree of malnutrition. This is the appropriate health maintenance response because early intervention helps prevent further medical deterioration and supports recovery.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Fluoxetine is not first-line treatment for anorexia nervosa and is not effective for acute weight restoration. Nutritional rehabilitation and close medical monitoring are needed first.

Psychotherapy alone is not adequate when anorexia nervosa is accompanied by abnormal vital signs and significant weight loss. She needs nutritional rehabilitation and medical follow-up, with possible escalation to inpatient care.

Although intense exercise can contribute to menstrual delay, this patient has substantial weight loss, restrictive eating, a very low BMI, bradycardia, and hypotension. These findings require active treatment rather than reassurance and observation.

Continuing sports participation is unsafe in a patient with significant weight loss, bradycardia, and hypotension. Routine dietary counseling alone is insufficient for suspected anorexia nervosa with medical instability.

questions.teaching_point: Adolescents with anorexia nervosa require early recognition of medical instability. Management focuses on nutritional rehabilitation, stopping excessive exercise, family-based or multidisciplinary therapy, and urgent escalation of care when vital signs or malnutrition suggest possible need for hospitalization.

questions.vignette: A 2-week-old boy is brought to clinic because of poor feeding, sweating with feeds, and slow weight gain. He was born at term without complications, and the pregnancy history is unremarkable. His mother says his lips sometimes look slightly blue when he cries. On exam, the infant is tachypneic with mild retractions. Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Cardiac exam reveals a single loud S2, a systolic murmur along the left sternal border, and bounding peripheral pulses. The liver edge is 3 cm below the right costal margin. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this infant's presentation?

answer_choices.text: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Tetralogy of Fallot
Transposition of the great arteries
Truncus arteriosus
Ventricular septal defect

questions.rationale: Truncus arteriosus is the best diagnosis because it causes early cyanosis together with signs of congestive heart failure as pulmonary blood flow increases after birth. A single arterial trunk supplies the systemic, pulmonary, and coronary circulations, and the associated ventricular septal defect produces a systolic murmur. The combination of a single loud S2, bounding pulses, hepatomegaly, tachypnea, low oxygen saturation, cardiomegaly, and increased pulmonary vascular markings is classic for truncus arteriosus.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return can cause cyanosis and respiratory distress, especially with obstructed drainage, but it more often presents with pulmonary edema and severe respiratory compromise rather than bounding pulses and the single loud S2 expected with truncus arteriosus.

Tetralogy of Fallot usually causes cyanosis from decreased pulmonary blood flow and classically has a harsh systolic ejection murmur with pulmonary oligemia on chest radiograph, not bounding pulses and increased pulmonary vascular markings.

Transposition of the great arteries causes early cyanosis, but it typically has minimal findings on auscultation and does not usually produce bounding pulses and pulmonary overcirculation with cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings in the first days to weeks of life.

An isolated ventricular septal defect can cause a systolic murmur, tachypnea, poor feeding, and heart failure, but it does not usually cause cyanosis or a single loud S2, making it less consistent with this presentation.

questions.teaching_point: Truncus arteriosus presents in early infancy with cyanosis plus heart failure signs, often with a single S2, a systolic murmur from the associated VSD, bounding pulses, and increased pulmonary vascular markings from excessive pulmonary blood flow.

questions.vignette: A 39-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 hours of heavy vaginal bleeding and worsening lower abdominal cramping. She reports months of progressively heavier menstrual periods, often passing large clots and needing to change pads every 1-2 hours during her cycle. She also feels fatigued and has noticed increasing pelvic pressure and urinary frequency. She is afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and her abdominal exam shows a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus. Pregnancy test is negative. Pelvic exam reveals active bleeding from the cervical os without cervical motion tenderness.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease
Ectopic pregnancy
Adenomyosis
Endometrial carcinoma
Uterine leiomyoma

questions.rationale: Uterine leiomyoma is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has classic symptoms of fibroids: heavy menstrual bleeding with clots, progressive bulk symptoms such as pelvic pressure and urinary frequency, and a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus on exam. In the emergency department, acute bleeding can occur from submucosal or larger fibroids even when the patient is hemodynamically stable.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease may present with pelvic pain and abnormal bleeding, but it typically includes cervical motion tenderness, fever, mucopurulent discharge, or adnexal tenderness rather than months of heavy cyclic bleeding and a firm, enlarged irregular uterus.

Ectopic pregnancy can present with vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain, but the negative pregnancy test makes this diagnosis unlikely. It also would not explain the chronic history of progressively heavy menses and uterine enlargement.
Adenomyosis can cause heavy painful menses and a boggy, uniformly enlarged uterus, but it does not usually produce the irregularly enlarged, firm uterus and bulk-related urinary symptoms seen here.

Endometrial carcinoma can cause abnormal uterine bleeding, but it is more concerning in postmenopausal patients or those with risk factors such as obesity, chronic anovulation, or unopposed estrogen. The enlarged irregular uterus and bulk symptoms are more suggestive of leiomyoma.

questions.teaching_point: Leiomyomas commonly cause heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and a firm irregularly enlarged uterus in reproductive-age patients.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man arrives to the emergency department 40 minutes after the sudden onset of severe, tearing chest pain that began while he was lifting a heavy box. The pain radiates to his back and is associated with diaphoresis and lightheadedness. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. On exam, he is anxious and pale; blood pressure is 182/96 mm Hg in the right arm and 156/88 mm Hg in the left arm. Radial pulses are diminished on the left compared with the right. He is alert, speaking in full sentences, and has no respiratory distress. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy without acute ST-segment elevation. Chest radiograph is normal.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Computed tomography angiography of the chest
Coronary angiography
Transthoracic echocardiography
Serial high-sensitivity troponin measurements
Ventilation-perfusion scan

questions.rationale: This patient has acute aortic dissection, suggested by abrupt tearing chest pain radiating to the back, blood pressure asymmetry, pulse deficit, and severe hypertension. Because he is hemodynamically stable enough for transport and does not have a known contraindication to iodinated contrast, computed tomography angiography of the chest is the best next study to confirm the diagnosis and define the extent of dissection. CTA is fast, widely available, and highly sensitive and specific for aortic dissection.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Coronary angiography is used to evaluate suspected coronary artery disease or acute coronary syndrome, not to confirm aortic dissection.

Transthoracic echocardiography can sometimes detect proximal aortic pathology, but it is less sensitive than CT angiography for confirming dissection and is not the preferred test in a stable patient.
Serial troponin measurements may help assess for acute coronary syndrome, but they do not confirm aortic dissection and could delay definitive imaging.

A ventilation-perfusion scan evaluates for pulmonary embolism, but this presentation is much more consistent with aortic dissection because of the tearing pain, inter-arm blood pressure difference, and diminished pulse on one side.

questions.teaching_point: In a stable patient with suspected aortic dissection, CT angiography of the chest is the preferred confirmatory study; echocardiography is mainly reserved for patients who are too unstable for CT or when CT cannot be performed.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man with a history of long-standing hypertension and cigarette smoking presents to the emergency department with abrupt onset of severe anterior chest pain that began while he was lifting boxes. He describes the pain as sharp and “tearing” and says it now radiates to his back. He is anxious and diaphoretic. Blood pressure is 182/96 mm Hg in the right arm and 156/88 mm Hg in the left arm; pulse is 112/min. Cardiac exam reveals a new early diastolic murmur. ECG shows nonspecific ST-T changes, and initial troponin is negative. Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. He is hemodynamically stable, and the team is considering the next study to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Transthoracic echocardiography
Transesophageal echocardiography
Computed tomography angiography of the chest with contrast
Radionuclide ventilation-perfusion scan
Serial cardiac troponins and ECGs

questions.rationale: Computed tomography angiography of the chest with contrast is the preferred confirmatory study in a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected aortic dissection. This patient has multiple high-risk features, including abrupt tearing chest pain, pain radiating to the back, pulse/BP differential between arms, a new diastolic murmur suggesting aortic regurgitation, and mediastinal widening on chest radiograph.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Transthoracic echocardiography may detect proximal aortic root disease or complications, but it is less sensitive for confirming dissection and is not the preferred definitive study here.
Transesophageal echocardiography can diagnose aortic dissection and is useful when CT is not feasible or the patient is unstable, but CTA is the best next confirmatory test in a stable patient.
A ventilation-perfusion scan is used to evaluate pulmonary embolism, but this presentation is more consistent with aortic dissection than thromboembolic disease.

Serial troponins and ECGs evaluate acute coronary syndrome, which can overlap symptomatically, but the blood pressure differential, mediastinal widening, and new murmur make dissection more likely and require immediate aortic imaging.

questions.teaching_point: In a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected aortic dissection, CT angiography of the chest with contrast is the best confirmatory test.

questions.vignette: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic because of 3 months of intermittent headaches and episodes of vomiting, usually in the early morning. His parents also report that he has become clumsier when running and has started veering to one side while walking. Over the past 2 weeks, he has had difficulty with handwriting and has begun holding books very close to read. On examination, his growth and vital signs are normal. He has mild truncal ataxia and an abnormal gait. Funduscopic examination shows blurred optic disc margins. There is no neck stiffness or fever.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding would be most consistent with the underlying lesion?

answer_choices.text: Facial weakness with loss of the corneal reflex
Resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity
Spasticity with hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response
Flaccid weakness with absent deep tendon reflexes
Ipsilateral limb dysmetria with an intention tremor on finger-to-nose testing

questions.rationale: This child has signs of increased intracranial pressure (early morning headache, vomiting, papilledema) plus cerebellar dysfunction (truncal ataxia, abnormal gait), which are typical of a posterior fossa mass such as a pilocytic astrocytoma in a child. Cerebellar lesions commonly cause ipsilateral limb incoordination, dysmetria, and intention tremor on finger-to-nose testing.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Facial weakness with loss of the corneal reflex suggests a pontine cranial nerve VII lesion, which is not the most likely localization here.
Resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity is characteristic of parkinsonism and does not fit a pediatric cerebellar tumor.
Spasticity, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response indicate an upper motor neuron/corticospinal tract lesion rather than a cerebellar lesion.
Flaccid weakness with absent reflexes indicates a lower motor neuron or peripheral nerve process, not a cerebellar/posterior fossa mass.

questions.teaching_point: Pilocytic astrocytoma in children often presents as a cerebellar/posterior fossa mass with increased intracranial pressure and cerebellar signs such as ataxia, dysmetria, and intention tremor.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old woman is admitted for acute pancreatitis due to gallstones. She has a history of compensated cirrhosis from prior hepatitis C infection and is improving with supportive care. She asks what vaccines she should receive before discharge. Her immunization record shows no prior hepatitis A vaccination. She does not drink alcohol and has no known immunocompromising condition.
questions.lead_in: Which preventive intervention is most appropriate regarding hepatitis A?

answer_choices.text: Administer the hepatitis B vaccine series instead
No hepatitis A prevention is indicated because she is not traveling
Defer hepatitis A vaccination until she develops abnormal liver enzymes
Administer hepatitis A immune globulin only
Administer the hepatitis A vaccine series before discharge

questions.rationale: Adults with chronic liver disease, including cirrhosis, should receive hepatitis A vaccination if they are not already immune. This patient is hospitalized for an unrelated condition and has a clear ACIP indication for hepatitis A immunization before discharge. Vaccination is preventive and appropriate even without travel history.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Hepatitis B vaccination may also be indicated for some adults with chronic liver disease, but the question asks specifically about hepatitis A prevention, for which the hepatitis A vaccine is the correct intervention.
Travel is only one of several indications for hepatitis A vaccination. Chronic liver disease is an independent indication, so prevention is appropriate even without travel plans.
Waiting for abnormal liver enzymes is inappropriate. Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended based on risk status before infection occurs, not after liver injury develops.

Immune globulin is reserved for select postexposure prophylaxis situations or for some travelers who cannot receive vaccine; it is not the routine preventive strategy for an unvaccinated adult with chronic liver disease.

questions.teaching_point: Adults with chronic liver disease should receive hepatitis A vaccination as preventive care, regardless of travel history.

questions.vignette: A 49-year-old man is seen in clinic for fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance, and dull pain in both second and third MCP joints. He also reports decreased libido over the past year. He has a family history of “liver disease” in his father. Exam shows mild hepatomegaly and bronze discoloration of the skin. Laboratory studies show ferritin 980 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 72%, and mildly elevated AST and ALT. Hepatitis serologies are negative. He is hemodynamically stable and has no signs of heart failure or decompensated liver disease.
questions.lead_in: Which intervention is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Refer for liver transplantation evaluation
Initiate therapeutic phlebotomy on a regular schedule
Order MRI of the liver to quantify hepatic iron before starting treatment
Begin oral deferasirox therapy
Start iron supplementation to correct presumed anemia

questions.rationale: This patient has hereditary hemochromatosis, suggested by the classic combination of fatigue, arthralgias of the second and third MCP joints, decreased libido, bronze skin pigmentation, hepatomegaly, elevated ferritin, and increased transferrin saturation. In a stable outpatient without decompensated liver disease or severe anemia, the first-line treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy. Repeated phlebotomy lowers total body iron stores and helps prevent progression to cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and hypogonadism. Iron studies are already diagnostic here, so additional imaging is not needed before treatment.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Liver transplantation is considered only for end-stage liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma, not as the initial treatment for stable iron overload.

MRI can help assess hepatic iron burden when the diagnosis is uncertain or to stage disease, but this patient already has a classic presentation and biochemical evidence of iron overload. Treatment should not be delayed to obtain MRI.
Iron chelation with deferasirox is reserved for patients who cannot undergo phlebotomy or for transfusional iron overload. It is not first-line therapy for uncomplicated hereditary hemochromatosis.
Iron supplementation would worsen iron overload and is contraindicated in a patient with hereditary hemochromatosis.

questions.teaching_point: Stable patients with hereditary hemochromatosis should be treated first-line with serial therapeutic phlebotomy to remove excess iron and prevent end-organ damage.

questions.vignette: A 67-year-old man with hypertension and a prior myocardial infarction reports 3 months of worsening shortness of breath when climbing one flight of stairs and occasional waking at night gasping for air. He has mild bilateral ankle swelling by evening and has gained 4 kg over the past 2 months. Blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg, heart rate is 92/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Cardiac exam reveals an S3 gallop and mildly elevated jugular venous pressure. Lung exam shows faint bibasilar crackles. He has no chest pain or fever. He is seen in clinic for evaluation of suspected chronic heart failure.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected diagnosis and help guide subsequent management?

answer_choices.text: Cardiac stress testing
12-lead electrocardiography
Transthoracic echocardiography
Chest radiography
Coronary angiography

questions.rationale: Transthoracic echocardiography is the key outpatient diagnostic study for suspected chronic heart failure. It confirms the presence of structural or functional cardiac abnormalities, including reduced or preserved ejection fraction, chamber enlargement, valvular disease, and diastolic dysfunction, and it helps direct guideline-based therapy.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Stress testing may be appropriate if ischemia is suspected as an underlying cause, but it is not the best next study to confirm heart failure in this presentation.
An electrocardiogram is useful as an initial part of the evaluation, but it does not confirm heart failure or characterize cardiac function as well as echocardiography.
Chest radiography can show pulmonary congestion or cardiomegaly, but it is insufficient to confirm heart failure or define left ventricular function.

Coronary angiography is invasive and reserved for patients in whom ischemic heart disease is strongly suspected or when noninvasive testing indicates a need for further evaluation; it is not first-line for confirming heart failure.

questions.teaching_point: In stable outpatients with suspected heart failure, transthoracic echocardiography is the most important study to confirm the diagnosis and determine ejection fraction and structural abnormalities.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man comes to an urgent care clinic with a sudden severe headache that began 2 hours ago while he was gardening. He has nausea, has vomited once, and says the pain reached maximum intensity within minutes. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and has hypertension that is often poorly controlled. He denies recent illness or head trauma. On exam, he is alert but uncomfortable; blood pressure is 198/104 mm Hg, heart rate is 88/min, and temperature is normal. He has no neck stiffness and no eye pain.
questions.lead_in: Which additional finding would be most concerning for an acute intracranial hemorrhage rather than a primary headache disorder?

answer_choices.text: Headache that is similar to prior episodes and improves with rest in a dark room
Headache preceded by flashing lights and followed by a unilateral throbbing headache
A new unilateral arm weakness with facial droop
Headache with tearing of one eye and unilateral nasal congestion
Pain that is bilateral, bandlike, and worsens with prolonged desk work

questions.rationale: New focal neurologic deficits, such as unilateral arm weakness with facial droop, are highly concerning for an acute structural intracranial process, including intracranial hemorrhage. In this patient, the thunderclap onset, severe hypertension, and apixaban use further increase concern for bleeding and warrant urgent neuroimaging. Primary headache disorders may cause severe pain and associated symptoms, but they do not typically produce new focal motor deficits.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A headache that is similar to prior episodes and improves with rest in a dark room is more consistent with migraine than with a new intracranial hemorrhage.
Visual aura followed by a unilateral throbbing headache is typical of migraine and supports a primary headache disorder rather than intracranial hemorrhage.
Unilateral eye tearing and nasal congestion suggest cluster headache, a primary headache disorder, rather than intracranial hemorrhage.
A bilateral, bandlike headache worsened by prolonged desk work is most consistent with tension-type headache, not acute intracranial bleeding.

questions.teaching_point: Thunderclap headache in an older adult taking anticoagulation and with severe hypertension should raise concern for intracranial hemorrhage; new focal neurologic deficits are especially alarming and require immediate evaluation.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man presents for follow-up of type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 6 years ago. He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily and walks regularly. He does not have known coronary artery disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease. Over the past 4 months, his home glucose readings have been fasting in the 170-190 mg/dL range. His A1c is 8.4%, unchanged from 3 months ago. He is 92 kg with a BMI of 33 kg/m2. Blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL and eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m2. He asks about adding a medication that could help improve glycemic control and support weight loss.
questions.lead_in: Which medication should be added next?

answer_choices.text: Start regular insulin
Add pioglitazone
Add semaglutide
Add glyburide
Switch metformin to sitagliptin

questions.rationale: Semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, is the best next medication to add for this patient with type 2 diabetes that remains above goal on metformin and with obesity. GLP-1 receptor agonists lower A1c effectively and promote weight loss with a low risk of hypoglycemia, making them especially appropriate when weight reduction is a treatment goal. Compared with the other options, semaglutide offers better weight benefit than sitagliptin, glyburide, or pioglitazone, and it is preferable to starting insulin in this stable outpatient with only moderately elevated A1c.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Regular insulin is not the preferred next step in a stable outpatient with moderately elevated A1c on oral therapy. It carries a higher risk of hypoglycemia and weight gain and is usually reserved for more severe hyperglycemia or failure of noninsulin options.
Pioglitazone can improve insulin sensitivity, but it often causes weight gain and fluid retention. It does not match the patient’s goal of supporting weight loss.
Glyburide can reduce glucose, but it commonly causes hypoglycemia and weight gain, which makes it a poor choice for an overweight patient who would benefit from weight loss.

Sitagliptin may lower A1c modestly, but it is generally weight neutral and less effective for weight loss than a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Metformin is already tolerated and should not be switched away from in this setting.

questions.teaching_point: In overweight adults with type 2 diabetes who remain above A1c goal on metformin, a GLP-1 receptor agonist such as semaglutide is often preferred because it improves glycemic control, supports weight loss, and has a low hypoglycemia risk.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old man comes to a primary care clinic in late winter with 1 day of worsening headache, fever, nausea, and photophobia. He returned from a crowded work conference 3 days ago. He has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications. Temperature is 39.1 C (102.4 F), heart rate is 112/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. On examination, he is alert but uncomfortable. He has marked neck stiffness and pain with passive flexion of the neck. A CT scan of the head performed before lumbar puncture shows no mass effect. Cerebrospinal fluid later shows increased opening pressure, neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and elevated protein.
questions.lead_in: Which underlying pathophysiologic process best explains this patient's cerebrospinal fluid findings?

answer_choices.text: Autoimmune demyelination of the central nervous system causing lymphocytic inflammation
Viral replication within meningeal cells leading to isolated lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose
Subarachnoid hemorrhage with secondary meningeal irritation and xanthochromic cerebrospinal fluid
Acute invasion of the subarachnoid space by pyogenic bacteria triggering neutrophilic inflammation
Chronic fungal infection of the meninges causing predominantly lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein and low glucose

questions.rationale: Acute bacterial meningitis occurs when pyogenic bacteria invade the subarachnoid space and provoke a strong inflammatory response. Neutrophils migrate into the cerebrospinal fluid, blood-brain barrier permeability increases, opening pressure rises, protein increases, and glucose falls because of bacterial and leukocyte metabolism. This pattern matches the patient's cerebrospinal fluid findings.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Autoimmune demyelinating disorders affect white matter and do not produce the acute febrile meningeal syndrome with neutrophilic cerebrospinal fluid, low glucose, and elevated protein seen here.
Most viral meningitides cause lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and only mildly elevated protein, which does not fit this patient's cerebrospinal fluid profile.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage can cause headache, neck stiffness, and xanthochromic or bloody cerebrospinal fluid, but it does not classically cause febrile illness with neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose.

Chronic fungal meningitis can cause lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose, but it usually has a more subacute course and does not typically present with the marked neutrophilic pattern described here.

questions.teaching_point: Acute bacterial meningitis causes neutrophilic cerebrospinal fluid with low glucose, high protein, and elevated opening pressure because bacteria invade the subarachnoid space and trigger intense inflammation.

questions.vignette: A 14-year-old boy with end-stage renal disease from congenital reflux nephropathy is admitted for pneumonia. He receives hemodialysis three times weekly through a tunneled right internal jugular catheter. This morning he is afebrile and hemodynamically stable, but his nursing note reports a new dressing with scant blood and the dialysis nurse cannot aspirate blood from the catheter and meets resistance when flushing, even after the patient is repositioned. The line is positional and sluggish, and he is due for dialysis today. The catheter exit site has no erythema, warmth, or purulent drainage. His father asks whether the line can still be used because the child feels fine.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding the dialysis catheter?

answer_choices.text: Remove the catheter immediately and place a new tunneled catheter later today
Proceed with dialysis using the catheter as is because the patient is asymptomatic
Administer tissue plasminogen activator to the catheter lumen and reassess function
Apply a topical antibiotic ointment to the exit site and use the line as scheduled
Obtain blood cultures from the catheter and start empiric vancomycin

questions.rationale: The most appropriate next step is to treat likely catheter thrombosis or fibrin sheath dysfunction with a thrombolytic instilled into the catheter lumen, such as tissue plasminogen activator, and then reassess patency. The catheter is malfunctioning because blood cannot be aspirated and flushing meets resistance despite repositioning, but there are no signs of exit-site infection or catheter-related bloodstream infection. In a child who depends on hemodialysis access, restoring catheter function is preferred before removing or replacing the line.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Immediate catheter removal is reserved for severe infection, persistent bacteremia, or a catheter that cannot be salvaged. This catheter appears obstructed rather than infected, so a declotting attempt is the appropriate first step.

Dialysis should not proceed through a catheter that cannot aspirate blood and resists flushing, because this suggests significant dysfunction and risks inadequate dialysis or catheter damage. The line needs to be evaluated and treated for suspected thrombotic obstruction first.

Topical antibiotic ointment is used for selected exit-site infections, but this catheter has no erythema, warmth, or drainage. Ointment would not correct the inability to aspirate or flush the catheter.

Blood cultures and empiric vancomycin are appropriate when catheter infection is suspected, such as with fever, hemodynamic instability, or local inflammatory findings. This patient is afebrile and the problem described is mechanical catheter dysfunction, not infection.

questions.teaching_point: In a hemodialysis patient with catheter dysfunction but no evidence of infection, the first management step is to address likely thrombotic obstruction with declotting therapy and reassessment of catheter patency.

questions.vignette: A 2-day-old male infant is noted to have persistent cyanosis shortly after birth. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Oxygen saturation remains 78% despite supplemental oxygen. On examination, he has a single second heart sound, a systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, and mild tachypnea. Chest radiograph shows decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
questions.lead_in: Which congenital heart defect is most likely?

answer_choices.text: Patent ductus arteriosus
Transposition of the great arteries
Ventricular septal defect
Tricuspid atresia
Tetralogy of Fallot

questions.rationale: Tricuspid atresia causes cyanotic congenital heart disease because blood cannot flow normally from the right atrium to the right ventricle, leading to obligate right-to-left shunting at the atrial level. Newborns often present with persistent hypoxemia that does not correct with oxygen, a single S2, a murmur from associated shunting, and decreased pulmonary vascular markings if pulmonary blood flow is reduced.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus is usually acyanotic initially and is associated with a continuous machine-like murmur and increased pulmonary blood flow rather than persistent neonatal cyanosis with decreased pulmonary vascular markings.

Transposition of the great arteries causes severe neonatal cyanosis, but the chest radiograph more often shows increased pulmonary vascularity and a narrow mediastinum rather than decreased pulmonary markings.
A ventricular septal defect typically causes a left-to-right shunt and presents with a holosystolic murmur and pulmonary overcirculation, not early refractory cyanosis in a newborn.

Tetralogy of Fallot can also cause cyanosis and decreased pulmonary blood flow, but it is classically associated with a harsh systolic ejection murmur and episodic hypercyanotic spells rather than the exam pattern of a single S2 from absent right-sided AV inflow.

questions.teaching_point: Tricuspid atresia is a cyanotic congenital heart defect in which absent tricuspid valve flow leads to right-to-left atrial shunting, persistent hypoxemia, and decreased pulmonary blood flow.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man is admitted after several weeks of worsening shortness of breath and difficulty clearing secretions. Over the past 8 months, he has developed progressive weakness in both hands and has trouble turning doorknobs and buttoning shirts. He also reports frequent choking on liquids and a 12-lb unintentional weight loss. His wife notes that his speech has become slurred and that he occasionally laughs or cries at inappropriate times. He denies numbness, back pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or visual changes. Examination shows dysarthria, tongue fasciculations, diffuse muscle atrophy in the hands, bilateral hyperreflexia, and increased tone in the legs. Sensation is intact.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis is most likely?

answer_choices.text: Myasthenia gravis
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Primary progressive multiple sclerosis
Guillain-Barré syndrome

questions.rationale: This patient has a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome affecting both upper and lower motor neurons: distal weakness with muscle atrophy and fasciculations (lower motor neuron signs) plus hyperreflexia and increased tone (upper motor neuron signs), along with bulbar involvement causing dysarthria and dysphagia. Preserved sensation and the absence of bowel/bladder symptoms or a sensory level also support amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Respiratory decline and pseudobulbar affect further fit ALS.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Myasthenia gravis can cause bulbar weakness and dyspnea, but it does not cause upper motor neuron signs such as hyperreflexia or increased tone, and muscle atrophy/fasciculations are not typical early findings.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy can produce hand weakness and hyperreflexia, but it usually includes sensory changes, neck symptoms, or gait disturbance from spinal cord compression rather than diffuse bulbar dysfunction and widespread lower motor neuron findings.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis may cause progressive motor dysfunction, but sensory findings, visual symptoms, and demyelinating features are more typical, and it does not usually produce the classic combination of fasciculations, muscle atrophy, and bulbar lower motor neuron involvement seen here.

Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness and areflexia after a recent illness, often with sensory symptoms or autonomic instability. This patient instead has a chronic progressive course with hyperreflexia and mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.

questions.teaching_point: ALS causes progressive mixed upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction with bulbar weakness and preserved sensation.

questions.vignette: A 13-year-old girl is brought to an urgent care clinic by her mother for sudden right lower abdominal pain that began 6 hours ago while she was at dance practice. The pain is severe and constant, and she has vomited twice since it started. She had a similar, milder episode of pain last week that resolved on its own. She has not started menstruating yet. Temperature is 37.2 C (99.0 F), heart rate is 112/min, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Abdominal exam shows right lower quadrant tenderness without rebound or guarding. Pelvic ultrasound done earlier this month for intermittent abdominal discomfort showed a 5.5-cm simple right ovarian cyst.
questions.lead_in: Which additional historical feature most strongly supports the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Gradual bilateral lower abdominal cramping with heavy vaginal bleeding
Dysuria with urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort
Periumbilical pain that migrated to the right lower quadrant over 24 hours
Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain that has occurred in prior self-limited episodes, especially with nausea or vomiting
Pain that improves after passing gas and is associated with loose stools

questions.rationale: Ovarian torsion is suggested by sudden unilateral pelvic or lower abdominal pain, often with nausea and vomiting, and pain that may come and go if the ovary twists and untwists intermittently. A prior ovarian cyst increases the risk of torsion because adnexal masses can act as a lead point for twisting. In this patient, a history of recurrent self-limited unilateral pain with nausea or vomiting would be the most supportive additional feature.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Gradual bilateral cramping with heavy vaginal bleeding is more consistent with menstrual-related pain or abnormal uterine bleeding, not ovarian torsion.
Dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort suggest a urinary tract infection rather than torsion.
Migratory pain from the periumbilical area to the right lower quadrant over time is more consistent with appendicitis than ovarian torsion.
Pain relieved by passing gas with loose stools is more suggestive of a gastrointestinal cause such as gastroenteritis or bowel gas, not ovarian torsion.

questions.teaching_point: In children and adolescents, ovarian torsion should be suspected with sudden unilateral pelvic pain and nausea/vomiting, especially when pain has occurred in intermittent episodes or when an ovarian cyst is present.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old woman comes to clinic because of progressively worsening pain in both knees for 2 years. The pain is worse after gardening and climbing stairs and improves with rest. She has morning stiffness that lasts about 10 minutes. She has hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3 with an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73 m2. She tried oral ibuprofen from a neighbor with little relief and stopped it after noticing increased blood pressure at home. Exam shows bony enlargement and crepitus of both knees without warmth or effusion. She is asking what treatment is most appropriate next.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate evidence-based treatment to recommend next?

answer_choices.text: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injections
Allopurinol therapy
Long-term opioid therapy
Daily oral prednisone
Topical diclofenac gel applied to the knees

questions.rationale: Topical diclofenac is an evidence-based first-line pharmacologic option for knee osteoarthritis, especially in an adult with localized symptoms and comorbid chronic kidney disease and hypertension that make oral NSAIDs less desirable. It provides pain relief with lower systemic exposure than oral NSAIDs.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid may be considered in selected patients, but it is not the best next step here. Topical NSAID therapy is generally preferred first for localized knee osteoarthritis before procedural therapies.
Allopurinol is used for gout prevention, not osteoarthritis. This patient's chronic, activity-related knee pain with bony enlargement is more consistent with osteoarthritis than crystal arthritis.

Long-term opioid therapy is not recommended for routine osteoarthritis management because benefits are limited and risks include dependence, falls, and constipation; safer, effective options should be used first.
Oral prednisone is not an appropriate routine treatment for osteoarthritis and exposes the patient to unnecessary systemic adverse effects without addressing the underlying mechanical joint disease.

questions.teaching_point: For symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, topical NSAIDs are preferred when pain is localized, especially when oral NSAIDs are risky because of kidney disease, hypertension, or other comorbidities.

questions.vignette: A 15-year-old boy is brought to clinic for severe, recurring right-sided headaches for the past 3 weeks. Each attack begins abruptly, peaks within minutes, and lasts about 45 to 60 minutes. During episodes, he paces the room and cannot lie still. He has prominent tearing and redness of the right eye, nasal congestion, and a drooping eyelid on the same side. Over-the-counter ibuprofen has not helped. Neurologic examination between attacks is normal, and he has no fever, neck stiffness, or focal weakness.
questions.lead_in: Which treatment is the best next step to abort his headaches?

answer_choices.text: Daily propranolol for prophylaxis
Acetaminophen with codeine as needed
Intravenous metoclopramide with diphenhydramine
Oral sumatriptan at the first sign of pain
High-flow 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask during an attack

questions.rationale: This presentation is most consistent with cluster headache: short, excruciating unilateral attacks with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms and marked restlessness. The best abortive treatment is high-flow 100% oxygen delivered by nonrebreather mask during the attack. This works rapidly and is appropriate even in adolescents, although pediatric management is often extrapolated from adult data. Rapid-acting triptans, especially subcutaneous or intranasal sumatriptan, can also abort attacks, but oral sumatriptan is too slow for headaches that peak within minutes.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Propranolol is used for migraine prevention, not to abort an active cluster headache attack. Preventive therapy for cluster headache, when needed, more commonly includes agents such as verapamil.
Acetaminophen with codeine is not an effective abortive treatment for cluster headache and exposes the patient to opioid adverse effects and medication-overuse risk.

Metoclopramide with diphenhydramine is commonly used for migraine-associated nausea or refractory migraine, but it does not treat cluster headache effectively and is not the best abortive option here.

Sumatriptan can be used for acute cluster headache, but the oral route has a slow onset and is not a good choice for rapidly peaking attacks; subcutaneous or intranasal formulations are preferred if a triptan is used.

questions.teaching_point: Cluster headache attacks are aborted most effectively with high-flow 100% oxygen; oral medications are usually too slow for these brief, severe attacks.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man is admitted from the emergency department with sudden-onset severe chest pain that began while he was lifting a heavy box at home. He describes the pain as sharp and tearing, radiating to his back between the shoulder blades. He is diaphoretic and restless. Blood pressure is 182/96 mm Hg in the right arm and 156/90 mm Hg in the left arm. Heart rate is 108/min. Cardiac troponin is normal, and the ECG shows nonspecific ST-T changes. On examination, there is a new diastolic murmur at the right sternal border.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis in this hemodynamically stable patient?

answer_choices.text: Coronary angiography
Ventilation-perfusion scan
CT angiography of the chest and abdomen with intravenous contrast
Plain chest radiography
Transthoracic echocardiography

questions.rationale: This patient has features concerning for acute aortic dissection: abrupt tearing chest pain radiating to the back, blood pressure differential between arms, and a new diastolic murmur suggesting aortic regurgitation. In a hemodynamically stable patient, CT angiography with intravenous contrast is the preferred diagnostic study because it is rapid, widely available, and highly sensitive and specific for defining the extent of dissection.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Coronary angiography evaluates coronary artery disease or acute coronary syndrome, which is less likely here given the tearing pain, arm blood pressure discrepancy, and new aortic regurgitation murmur.
A ventilation-perfusion scan is used to assess for pulmonary embolism, but the presentation is more consistent with aortic dissection than thromboembolic disease.
Plain chest radiography may show a widened mediastinum or pleural effusion, but it cannot confirm aortic dissection and should not be relied on as the definitive diagnostic study.
Transthoracic echocardiography can help detect proximal aortic root involvement or pericardial effusion, but it is less sensitive than CT angiography for confirming dissection in a stable patient.

questions.teaching_point: In a stable patient with suspected aortic dissection, CT angiography with IV contrast is the preferred confirmatory test.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old woman comes to an outpatient clinic because she has felt "constantly on edge" for the past 9 months. She worries about her job performance, her children’s safety, finances, and minor symptoms in her body almost every day. She says she can usually identify a new concern as soon as one problem is resolved. She has difficulty falling asleep, feels fatigued during the day, and notes frequent muscle tension in her neck and jaw. She denies panic attacks, intrusive traumatic memories, compulsive rituals, periods of elevated mood, or substance use. Her primary care evaluation, including thyroid studies and complete blood count, is unrevealing.
questions.lead_in: Which underlying mechanism best explains this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Elevated mood with decreased need for sleep and increased goal-directed activity
Obsessions that are relieved by performing repetitive rituals
Excessive and persistent worry due to dysregulation of limbic and prefrontal neural circuits
Intrusive reexperiencing of a traumatic event with associated hyperarousal
Recurrent unexpected surges of autonomic activation triggered by misinterpreted bodily sensations

questions.rationale: This patient has generalized anxiety disorder, characterized by excessive worry occurring most days for at least 6 months, difficulty controlling the worry, and associated symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and muscle tension. The underlying concept is dysregulation of brain circuits involved in fear and worry, particularly interactions between limbic structures and the prefrontal cortex, leading to persistent excessive apprehension rather than brief episodic panic or trauma-related symptoms.

distractor_rationales.explanation: This describes mania, which features persistently elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, and increased energy or goal-directed activity. The patient’s symptoms reflect anxious worry and tension, not mood elevation.

This describes obsessive-compulsive disorder, in which intrusive obsessions are followed by compulsions performed to reduce distress. The patient reports worry about many life areas rather than intrusive obsessions or ritualistic behaviors.

This describes posttraumatic stress disorder, which requires exposure to a traumatic event followed by reexperiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal symptoms. No trauma-related trigger or reexperiencing symptoms are present here.

This describes panic disorder, in which sudden panic attacks are associated with intense autonomic symptoms and fear of their recurrence. The vignette instead describes chronic, pervasive worry without discrete unexpected attacks.

questions.teaching_point: Generalized anxiety disorder is driven by persistent, hard-to-control worry linked to limbic-prefrontal circuit dysregulation and is distinguished from panic, PTSD, mania, and OCD by its chronic, diffuse nature.

questions.vignette: A 42-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of 8 months of fatigue, constipation, and difficulty losing weight despite no major diet changes. She also reports cold intolerance and heavier menstrual periods. She has a history of vitiligo and says her mother takes thyroid hormone, though she is unsure why. Examination shows a pulse of 58/min, dry skin, and a diffusely enlarged, firm, nontender thyroid without nodules. Laboratory studies show elevated TSH and low free T4. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are positive.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
Graves disease
Thyroid hormone resistance
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Iodine deficiency goiter

questions.rationale: This patient has primary hypothyroidism with a painless, diffusely enlarged firm thyroid and autoimmune features (vitiligo, family history of thyroid disease) plus positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies, which is most consistent with Hashimoto thyroiditis. Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in adults in iodine-sufficient regions.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is typically painful and tender, often follows a viral illness, and usually has a transient hyperthyroid phase before hypothyroidism; this vignette describes chronic painless hypothyroidism.
Graves disease causes hyperthyroid symptoms such as weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, and tachycardia, often with diffuse goiter and ophthalmopathy, not elevated TSH with low free T4.

Thyroid hormone resistance usually presents with elevated thyroid hormone levels and nonsuppressed TSH, often without classic hypothyroid symptoms; this patient has biochemical primary hypothyroidism.

Iodine deficiency can cause goiter and hypothyroidism, but in an adult living in an iodine-sufficient setting with positive thyroid autoantibodies and autoimmune comorbidity, autoimmune thyroiditis is much more likely.

questions.teaching_point: Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune cause of primary hypothyroidism characterized by elevated TSH, low free T4, and positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies.

questions.vignette: A 3-week-old term infant is brought to the outpatient clinic because he has had poor weight gain and progressive abdominal distention. He passed meconium 72 hours after birth, and since then has had infrequent, small stools despite feeding well. His parents report intermittent vomiting, which is nonbilious, and he seems more comfortable after a large bowel movement. On examination, he has a distended abdomen and decreased stool in the rectal vault. After a rectal exam, he passes a large amount of foul-smelling stool.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate initial study to evaluate this infant’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Contrast enema
Rectal suction biopsy
Upper gastrointestinal series
Anorectal manometry
Abdominal ultrasound

questions.rationale: Contrast enema is the most appropriate initial study when Hirschsprung disease is suspected. This infant has delayed passage of meconium, progressive abdominal distention, constipation, and explosive stool after rectal stimulation, which are classic findings. Contrast enema can demonstrate a transition zone between the narrow distal aganglionic segment and the proximally dilated colon. Rectal suction biopsy is the confirmatory test, but contrast enema is a useful first study in the evaluation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Rectal suction biopsy is the definitive confirmatory test for Hirschsprung disease because it demonstrates absent ganglion cells, but it is not the initial study in the evaluation.
An upper gastrointestinal series is used to assess upper intestinal obstruction such as malrotation or volvulus, which does not best match this infant’s constipation-predominant presentation.

Anorectal manometry can support the diagnosis by showing failure of relaxation of the internal anal sphincter, but it is not the most appropriate initial study in a young infant with classic findings of Hirschsprung disease.
