Exam shows diffuse expiratory wheezing with prolonged expiratory phase and mild intercostal retractions. Peak expiratory flow is 55% of his personal best. He receives an initial nebulized albuterol treatment and reports partial improvement, but after 20 minutes he remains tachypneic with persistent wheezing and continued work of breathing.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Start oral prednisone only and discharge with close outpatient follow-up
Initiate inhaled corticosteroid controller therapy without additional acute treatment
Administer nebulized ipratropium bromide, repeat inhaled albuterol treatments, and give oral prednisone
Obtain a chest radiograph before giving further bronchodilator therapy
Give intravenous magnesium sulfate as the next isolated therapy

questions.rationale: This child has a moderate asthma exacerbation with incomplete response to initial short-acting beta-agonist therapy. In the emergency department, the appropriate next step is to intensify acute treatment by continuing repeated inhaled albuterol, adding inhaled ipratropium bromide, and starting a systemic corticosteroid such as oral prednisone. Ipratropium is helpful in children with moderate to severe exacerbations, and early systemic corticosteroids reduce hospitalization and relapse. Intravenous magnesium sulfate is generally reserved for patients with severe symptoms who do not improve adequately after standard inhaled bronchodilator therapy and systemic corticosteroids.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Oral prednisone alone is not sufficient because the child still has persistent tachypnea, wheezing, and increased work of breathing after initial albuterol. Discharge would be premature without additional acute bronchodilator therapy and clearer clinical improvement.

Controller therapy with inhaled corticosteroids is important for long-term asthma management, but it does not treat the current acute bronchospasm and respiratory distress in the emergency department.

A chest radiograph is not routinely needed in a typical asthma exacerbation that is responding incompletely but appropriately to bronchodilator therapy. Imaging is reserved for concern about pneumonia, pneumothorax, foreign body aspiration, or another atypical feature.

IV magnesium sulfate can be considered for severe exacerbations that remain refractory after initial inhaled bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids. It is not the best next isolated therapy here because standard acute bronchodilator therapy and a systemic steroid have not yet been fully implemented.

questions.teaching_point: Moderate to severe pediatric asthma exacerbations in the ED should be treated with repeated inhaled albuterol, early systemic corticosteroids, and addition of ipratropium when symptoms persist after initial bronchodilator therapy.

questions.vignette: A 79-year-old man with hypertension and prior myocardial infarction comes to the emergency department for worsening shortness of breath over 2 days. He reports orthopnea, waking up at night gasping for air, and swelling in both ankles. He has gained 4 kg over the past week despite taking his medications. On exam, his blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg, pulse is 104/min, respirations are 24/min, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. He has jugular venous distention, bibasilar crackles, and 2+ pitting edema to the shins. A chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and bilateral interstitial edema.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is most appropriate to help confirm the suspected cause of his acute dyspnea?

answer_choices.text: Spirometry with bronchodilator testing
Computed tomography pulmonary angiography
Serum troponin level
D-dimer assay
Brain natriuretic peptide level

questions.rationale: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is released in response to ventricular stretch and is useful in the emergency department when acute decompensated heart failure is suspected. In this patient, the progressive orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, volume overload on exam, hypoxemia, and pulmonary edema on chest radiograph already strongly suggest heart failure; BNP can support the diagnosis and help distinguish it from other causes of dyspnea.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Spirometry with bronchodilator testing evaluates obstructive lung disease, which does not fit the patient’s orthopnea, edema, JVD, and pulmonary edema on imaging.
CT pulmonary angiography is appropriate if pulmonary embolism is suspected, but this patient’s presentation is more consistent with volume overload from heart failure than acute PE.
Serum troponin may be helpful if acute coronary syndrome is suspected as a trigger or alternative diagnosis, but it does not confirm heart failure as the cause of dyspnea.
A D-dimer assay is used to help exclude pulmonary embolism in low- or intermediate-risk patients, but it is not the best study when the clinical picture already points to acute heart failure.

questions.teaching_point: In acute dyspnea with signs of volume overload, BNP is a useful adjunct test to support heart failure and distinguish it from other cardiopulmonary causes.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man is seen in clinic after an incidental finding on abdominal ultrasound performed for mild right-sided flank discomfort. He has a 25-pack-year smoking history and newly diagnosed hypertension. He denies dysuria, fever, or stone passage. Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria without pyuria. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrates a 5.6-cm solid enhancing mass in the upper pole of the right kidney, and the mass appears technically amenable to nephron-sparing resection. There is no evidence of renal vein invasion or metastatic disease on chest imaging. His creatinine level is normal, and he has two functioning kidneys. He asks about the best next step in management.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Percutaneous needle biopsy of the renal mass
Partial nephrectomy of the right kidney
Radical nephrectomy
Active surveillance with repeat imaging in 6 months
Cystoscopy

questions.rationale: This patient has a localized, solid enhancing renal mass consistent with renal cell carcinoma. The lesion is 5.6 cm, placing it in the T1b category (4 to 7 cm), and it is described as technically amenable to nephron-sparing surgery. In a surgically fit adult with normal renal function and a normal contralateral kidney, partial nephrectomy is preferred when feasible because it provides oncologic control while preserving renal function. Therefore, partial nephrectomy is the best next step in management.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Percutaneous biopsy is not usually the next step when imaging shows a classic enhancing solid renal mass and the patient is already an operative candidate. Biopsy is more useful when the diagnosis is uncertain or when the result would change management, such as before ablation or in a poor surgical candidate.

Radical nephrectomy is generally reserved for tumors that are not suitable for nephron-sparing surgery, are more locally advanced, or involve the renal vein or adjacent structures. Because this mass is described as amenable to partial nephrectomy, radical nephrectomy is not the best choice.

Active surveillance is generally reserved for very small renal masses, patients with substantial comorbidity or limited life expectancy, or those who are poor candidates for intervention. A 5.6-cm enhancing mass in an otherwise operable adult warrants definitive treatment.

Cystoscopy evaluates the lower urinary tract and may be part of a hematuria workup, but it does not treat or further define the clearly identified renal cortical mass. The primary problem is a suspected renal cell carcinoma on CT.

questions.teaching_point: Localized renal cell carcinoma in a surgically fit adult is usually managed with nephron-sparing surgery when feasible, especially for T1 tumors.

questions.vignette: A 56-year-old man comes to the clinic 5 days after laparoscopic abdominal surgery. He reports mild shortness of breath when walking up stairs and a dry cough. He has been spending most of the day in bed because moving increases incisional discomfort. He denies fever, pleuritic chest pain, or leg swelling. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. On lung examination, breath sounds are decreased at the left base with faint inspiratory crackles that improve after a few deep breaths. The remainder of the exam is unremarkable.
questions.lead_in: Which physical examination finding is most consistent with this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Unilateral pleuritic chest wall tenderness with a friction rub over the affected side
Increased tactile fremitus with egophony over a focal area of consolidation
Diminished breath sounds and fine crackles at the lung base that improve with deep inspiration
Diffuse expiratory wheezing that becomes louder with forced expiration
Hyperresonance to percussion with tracheal deviation away from the affected side

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has postoperative atelectasis from shallow breathing and decreased lung expansion after abdominal surgery. Typical findings include decreased breath sounds, basilar crackles, and partial improvement after deep breathing, coughing, or incentive spirometry. The symptoms are mild and occur in the context of recent surgery and reduced mobility, which supports atelectasis over pneumonia or other acute pulmonary processes.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pleural friction rub and reproducible chest wall tenderness are more consistent with pleurisy or musculoskeletal pain, neither of which best explains the postoperative basilar findings.
Increased tactile fremitus and egophony indicate lung consolidation, as seen with pneumonia, rather than atelectasis, which causes reduced air entry and diminished resonance.
Diffuse expiratory wheezing suggests an obstructive airway process such as asthma or COPD exacerbation, not postoperative alveolar collapse.
Hyperresonance with tracheal deviation away from the affected side is characteristic of a tension pneumothorax, which would usually cause more acute and severe respiratory distress.

questions.teaching_point: Postoperative atelectasis commonly presents with basilar decreased breath sounds and crackles that improve with deep breathing, coughing, and mobilization.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man is admitted for progressive weakness and difficulty swallowing. Over the past 10 months, he has developed frequent tripping, trouble opening jars, and worsening slurred speech. He has lost 14 lb despite a normal appetite. He denies sensory loss, diplopia, vertigo, bowel or bladder changes, and significant back pain. Examination shows diffuse muscle atrophy, fasciculations in the tongue and both forearms, brisk deep tendon reflexes in the upper and lower extremities, and an extensor plantar response bilaterally. Sensation is intact. Cranial nerves otherwise are normal. A recent brain MRI shows only chronic small-vessel ischemic changes, and cervical spine imaging does not show cord compression.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Myasthenia gravis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
Multifocal motor neuropathy
Guillain-Barré syndrome

questions.rationale: This patient has progressive, asymmetric motor weakness with both upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses) and lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, fasciculations), along with bulbar involvement and preserved sensation. The combination of upper and lower motor neuron findings without sensory deficits is most consistent with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Myasthenia gravis can cause bulbar weakness and dysarthria, but it typically causes fatigable weakness without upper motor neuron signs, fasciculations, or muscle atrophy, and reflexes are usually preserved.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy can produce gait difficulty and hyperreflexia, but it would not usually cause tongue fasciculations, diffuse lower motor neuron findings, or progressive bulbar symptoms with a normal sensory examination.

Multifocal motor neuropathy causes asymmetric distal weakness and can include fasciculations, but it is a peripheral motor neuropathy that spares upper motor neuron signs and typically does not cause bulbar symptoms.

Guillain-Barré syndrome causes acute ascending weakness with areflexia, often after an infectious trigger. It does not fit the chronic progressive course or the presence of hyperreflexia and Babinski signs.

questions.teaching_point: ALS is suggested by progressive motor weakness with both upper and lower motor neuron signs, preserved sensation, and bulbar involvement.

questions.vignette: An 82-year-old woman on the inpatient medicine service develops sudden right-sided lower abdominal pain while ambulating to the bathroom. She has had intermittent nausea since the pain began 2 hours ago and one episode of vomiting. She is postmenopausal and reports no vaginal bleeding or urinary symptoms. Her history includes a known 7-cm right ovarian cyst that was found incidentally 3 months ago; she missed outpatient follow-up. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), blood pressure is 148/84 mm Hg, pulse is 104/min, and respirations are 18/min. Abdominal examination shows focal right lower quadrant tenderness with mild guarding but no rebound. Pelvic examination reveals a tender, enlarged right adnexal mass.
questions.lead_in: Which finding is most consistent with the likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Postmenopausal bleeding with a firm, fixed pelvic mass and weight loss
Migratory right lower quadrant pain with anorexia and maximal tenderness at McBurney point
Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with microscopic hematuria
Sudden-onset unilateral pelvic pain with nausea and a tender adnexal mass
Gradually worsening lower abdominal pain with fever and cervical motion tenderness

questions.rationale: This patient’s abrupt unilateral pelvic pain, nausea/vomiting, and tender enlarged adnexal mass in the setting of a known ovarian cyst are most consistent with ovarian torsion. A preexisting ovarian cyst or mass increases the risk of twisting of the ovary on its vascular pedicle, causing ischemic pain and gastrointestinal symptoms. Ovarian torsion is a gynecologic emergency; prompt pelvic ultrasound with Doppler and urgent surgical management are indicated.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding, a firm fixed pelvic mass, and weight loss are concerning for gynecologic malignancy, but they do not explain the abrupt unilateral pain, nausea, and adnexal tenderness typical of torsion.
Migratory pain that localizes to the right lower quadrant with anorexia and maximal tenderness at McBurney point is more consistent with appendicitis than with adnexal torsion.
Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with microscopic hematuria suggests nephrolithiasis, which does not cause a tender enlarged adnexal mass on pelvic examination.
Fever, cervical motion tenderness, and gradually worsening pain are more consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease or another infectious pelvic process than with sudden ovarian torsion.

questions.teaching_point: Suspect ovarian torsion when a patient has sudden unilateral pelvic pain, nausea/vomiting, and an adnexal mass, especially with a known ovarian cyst or mass; it is a surgical emergency.

questions.vignette: A 6-month-old boy is admitted after his mother reports that he has been increasingly sleepy and feeding poorly since a fall from a couch 2 days ago. He has had two episodes of vomiting and is difficult to arouse for feeds. Exam shows a full anterior fontanelle, intermittent irritability, and a left-sided pupil that is slightly larger than the right and reacts more slowly to light. His heart rate is 58/min, blood pressure is 92/54 mm Hg, and respirations are irregular. A noncontrast head CT shows a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection over the right cerebral hemisphere with mild midline shift.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Obtain a brain MRI with and without contrast before initiating treatment
Administer an osmotic agent and arrange emergent neurosurgical consultation
Begin high-dose corticosteroids to reduce cerebral edema
Start levetiracetam and observe for neurologic improvement on the pediatric ward
Perform a lumbar puncture to evaluate for infection

questions.rationale: This infant has a subdural hemorrhage with clinical evidence of increased intracranial pressure and impending herniation (decreased responsiveness, vomiting, full fontanelle, anisocoria, bradycardia, and irregular respirations). The immediate priority is stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation as needed, followed by urgent measures to lower intracranial pressure (such as hypertonic saline or mannitol, depending on local protocol and clinical status) and emergent neurosurgical consultation for definitive management. Additional testing should not delay treatment in a child with CT-confirmed hemorrhage and signs of neurologic deterioration.

distractor_rationales.explanation: MRI can provide more detail, but it should not delay urgent treatment in a child with CT-confirmed hemorrhage and signs of increased intracranial pressure.
High-dose corticosteroids are not recommended for acute management of subdural hemorrhage or elevated intracranial pressure from intracranial bleeding.

Antiseizure therapy may be used if seizures occur or for selected prophylaxis, but observation alone is inappropriate because this child already has signs of worsening intracranial pressure and requires urgent intervention.
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated because the child has intracranial mass effect and signs of increased intracranial pressure, which raises the risk of precipitating herniation.

questions.teaching_point: A child with subdural hemorrhage plus signs of increased intracranial pressure needs immediate ICP-lowering measures and emergent neurosurgical evaluation; do not delay care for lumbar puncture or further imaging.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man presents to his primary care clinician for 8 months of progressively worsening hand weakness. He has difficulty buttoning shirts and turning keys, and he has noticed twitching in his forearms and calves. He denies numbness, vision changes, dizziness, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. Examination shows asymmetric weakness in the hands and feet, diffuse muscle atrophy, and fasciculations. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk in the arms and legs. Sensation is intact.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis is most likely?

answer_choices.text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Peripheral neuropathy
Multiple sclerosis
Polymyositis
Myasthenia gravis

questions.rationale: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis causes progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons. The combination of asymmetric distal weakness, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and brisk reflexes with preserved sensation is classic for ALS in an outpatient adult with progressive functional decline.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Peripheral neuropathy can cause distal weakness, but it usually includes sensory symptoms such as numbness, paresthesias, or loss of sensation and does not produce brisk reflexes or a combined upper and lower motor neuron pattern.

Multiple sclerosis can produce upper motor neuron findings and neurologic deficits, but the typical course includes sensory symptoms, visual complaints, or episodic neurologic events rather than progressive motor-only weakness with fasciculations and muscle atrophy.

Polymyositis causes proximal muscle weakness due to inflammatory myopathy and usually does not produce fasciculations, marked muscle atrophy, or brisk reflexes; sensation remains intact, but the pattern of weakness is different.

Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness that typically worsens with use and improves with rest, often involving ocular or bulbar muscles; it does not cause muscle atrophy, fasciculations, or upper motor neuron signs.

questions.teaching_point: ALS is suggested by progressive asymmetric weakness with both upper motor neuron signs and lower motor neuron signs while sensation remains intact.

questions.vignette: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department for intermittent episodes of severe crying and drawing his legs up to his abdomen that began earlier today. Between episodes, he appears unusually tired but consolable. His parents report two episodes of vomiting. He had a mild upper respiratory infection last week. On examination, his abdomen is soft but he winces when the right lower quadrant is palpated, and a tubular mass is felt in the right upper abdomen.
questions.lead_in: Which associated finding is most consistent with this child's diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Intermittent colicky abdominal pain with periods of lethargy between episodes
Sudden diffuse abdominal rigidity with rebound tenderness after perforation
Progressive abdominal distention with bilious vomiting and absent bowel sounds
Pain that starts around the umbilicus and then localizes to the right lower quadrant with voluntary guarding
Blood-streaked emesis with pain relieved by feeding and poor weight gain

questions.rationale: This child’s episodic severe crying, leg-drawing, vomiting, and lethargy between episodes are most consistent with intussusception, in which one segment of bowel telescopes into another and causes intermittent obstruction and ischemia. A classic associated feature is recurrent colicky abdominal pain with periods of relative quietness or lethargy between painful episodes. The palpable abdominal mass described in the stem also supports this diagnosis, even without using the classic stool finding.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Diffuse rigidity and rebound tenderness indicate peritonitis from perforation, which is a different acute surgical emergency and not the usual associated finding in uncomplicated intussusception.
This is more consistent with a bowel obstruction or volvulus, which usually causes more persistent vomiting and progressive distention rather than intermittent pain with symptom-free intervals.

This describes appendicitis, which typically begins with periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant and produces more continuous localized tenderness rather than brief recurrent episodes.
This suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which classically causes nonbilious projectile vomiting, hunger after feeds, and poor weight gain, not episodic colicky pain or lethargy between attacks.

questions.teaching_point: In infants, intussusception is suggested by intermittent colicky abdominal pain, lethargy between episodes, vomiting, and sometimes a palpable abdominal mass; classic stool changes may appear later.

questions.vignette: A 76-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to an urgent care clinic because of 2 days of worsening fatigue, nausea, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. He has been drinking water but has not been able to keep food down. He takes metformin and basal insulin, but he missed several insulin doses after developing a urinary tract infection last week. He appears dehydrated, has dry mucous membranes, and is mildly tachypneic. Fingerstick glucose is 468 mg/dL. Urinalysis from a voided specimen shows large ketones and glucosuria. The clinician is concerned about diabetic ketoacidosis.
questions.lead_in: Which additional study is most appropriate to evaluate this patient for diabetic ketoacidosis and assess its severity?

answer_choices.text: Random serum cortisol level
Serum C-peptide level
Oral glucose tolerance test
Basic metabolic panel with serum bicarbonate and anion gap
Venous blood gas

questions.rationale: A basic metabolic panel is the most appropriate additional study because suspected diabetic ketoacidosis requires assessment of the serum bicarbonate, anion gap, potassium, and renal function. In this patient, the combination of marked hyperglycemia, dehydration, ketonuria, and tachypnea makes DKA likely, and the metabolic panel helps confirm a high anion gap metabolic acidosis and determine the severity of electrolyte abnormalities that will guide urgent treatment. Although a venous blood gas can also help document acidemia, the basic metabolic panel is the best single study listed for initial evaluation and severity assessment.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A random cortisol level is not part of the initial evaluation for suspected DKA unless there is a separate concern for adrenal insufficiency; it does not assess the acidosis, ketosis, or electrolyte abnormalities driving this presentation.
Serum C-peptide can help evaluate endogenous insulin production in selected diabetes workups, but it is not useful for diagnosing or staging an acute hyperglycemic emergency.
An oral glucose tolerance test is used to diagnose impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes in stable patients, not to evaluate an acutely ill patient with suspected ketoacidosis.

A venous blood gas can document acidemia and help evaluate DKA, but by itself it does not provide the full electrolyte assessment needed to gauge severity and guide immediate management as well as a basic metabolic panel does.

questions.teaching_point: When DKA is suspected, obtain serum chemistries to assess the anion gap, bicarbonate, potassium, and renal function; these data help confirm the diagnosis and determine immediate treatment needs.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his wife found him increasingly confused and unable to speak clearly over the past hour. He has hypertension and atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban. Earlier today he complained of a sudden, severe headache while sitting at breakfast, then became nauseated and vomited once. On arrival, he is drowsy but arousable, has a blood pressure of 198/108 mm Hg, and is not following commands reliably. Physical examination shows left-sided weakness and a rightward gaze preference. His pupils are equal and reactive, and he has no neck stiffness.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding would most strongly support intracranial hemorrhage as the cause of his acute neurologic deterioration?

answer_choices.text: Painful vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution
Asterixis with bilateral lower-extremity edema
Resting tremor that improves with intentional movement
Papilledema with worsening level of consciousness
Horizontal nystagmus that fatigues with gaze fixation

questions.rationale: Papilledema with worsening consciousness suggests increased intracranial pressure from an acute intracranial process such as hemorrhage. In this patient, the abrupt severe headache, vomiting, focal neurologic deficit, markedly elevated blood pressure, and altered mental status already raise strong concern for intracranial bleeding; evidence of raised intracranial pressure further supports that diagnosis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A painful vesicular dermatomal rash suggests herpes zoster and may cause localized neuropathic pain, but it does not account for the acute global neurologic deterioration and focal deficits seen here.

Asterixis and peripheral edema suggest metabolic encephalopathy or systemic disease such as hepatic or renal failure, which would not explain the sudden thunderclap headache, unilateral weakness, and gaze deviation.

A resting tremor that improves with intentional movement is typical of Parkinson disease and does not fit an abrupt presentation with severe headache, vomiting, and focal neurologic findings in the emergency setting.

Fatigable horizontal nystagmus with gaze fixation is more consistent with a peripheral vestibular process such as benign paroxysmal positional vertigo or vestibular neuritis, not an intracranial hemorrhage causing acute focal deficits and decreased responsiveness.

questions.teaching_point: Sudden severe headache with vomiting, focal neurologic deficits, and altered mental status should raise concern for intracranial hemorrhage; signs of increased intracranial pressure further support the diagnosis.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old woman is evaluated in clinic after an incidental finding of hypercalcemia on routine labs. She reports constipation and vague fatigue for several months but no acute symptoms. Repeat testing shows serum calcium 11.4 mg/dL, intact PTH elevated, creatinine normal, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D replete. She has no history of kidney stones, fragility fractures, or thiazide use. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry shows osteoporosis at the distal radius with a T-score of -2.7, but she remains physically active and has no focal bone pain. She asks what the best next step is to address her condition.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

answer_choices.text: Start cinacalcet therapy
Observe without treatment and repeat calcium in 1 year
Begin alendronate therapy
Refer for parathyroidectomy
Increase oral calcium supplementation

questions.rationale: This patient has primary hyperparathyroidism with a guideline-based indication for surgery: osteoporosis at a cortical site (distal radius) with a T-score of -2.7. In patients who are appropriate operative candidates, parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment and is recommended when there is skeletal involvement meeting osteoporosis criteria, nephrolithiasis, reduced renal function, significant hypercalcemia, or age younger than 50 years. Her mild hypercalcemia and nonspecific symptoms support the diagnosis, but the operative indication here is the documented osteoporosis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cinacalcet can lower serum calcium, but it is typically used when surgery is not possible, not desired, or as a bridge; it is not the preferred definitive treatment for an operative candidate.
Observation is reserved for selected patients who do not meet surgical criteria. This patient does meet criteria because she has osteoporosis on bone density testing.
Alendronate can improve bone density, but it does not correct the underlying parathyroid disorder or resolve the hypercalcemia, so it is not the best next step when surgery is indicated.
Increasing calcium supplementation would not treat the excess parathyroid hormone secretion and may worsen hypercalcemia.

questions.teaching_point: Primary hyperparathyroidism is treated definitively with parathyroidectomy when guideline criteria are met, including osteoporosis on DXA, kidney stones, renal impairment, marked hypercalcemia, or age younger than 50 years.

questions.vignette: A 67-year-old man comes to clinic because of 9 months of progressive slowness and stiffness. His wife says he has been “shuffling” more, needs extra time to get out of a chair, and has started writing much smaller than before. He also reports constipation and a reduced sense of smell over the past few years. He takes no dopamine-blocking medications. On examination, he has a masked facial expression, decreased arm swing on the right, and a resting tremor of the right hand that lessens when he reaches for a cup. Strength is normal, but rapid alternating movements are slow and decrement in amplitude on the right.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding is most likely in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Sensory loss in a stocking-glove distribution with absent ankle reflexes
Cogwheel rigidity with a bradykinetic gait
Proximal muscle weakness with preservation of reflexes
Spasticity with hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response
Intention tremor with dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing

questions.rationale: This patient has classic parkinsonian features: asymmetric resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, masked facies, reduced arm swing, micrographia, constipation, and hyposmia. A common associated examination finding is cogwheel rigidity and a bradykinetic, shuffling gait with reduced arm swing and en bloc turning.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Stocking-glove sensory loss with absent ankle reflexes suggests peripheral neuropathy, which can cause gait instability but does not explain the resting tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity seen here.
Proximal muscle weakness with preserved reflexes is more consistent with a myopathic process such as polymyalgia rheumatica or inflammatory myopathy, not a parkinsonian movement disorder.
Spasticity, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response indicate an upper motor neuron process such as stroke, cervical myelopathy, or multiple sclerosis, not Parkinson disease.
Intention tremor and dysmetria suggest cerebellar disease rather than Parkinson disease. Parkinsonian tremor is typically a resting tremor that improves with action.

questions.teaching_point: Parkinson disease is a clinical diagnosis characterized by bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity, often with masked facies, micrographia, and reduced arm swing.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of widespread bruising and gum bleeding that began 3 days ago. She had a viral upper respiratory illness 2 weeks ago but is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. She has no fever, confusion, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Vital signs are normal. Exam shows scattered petechiae over the lower extremities and bleeding at the gums, but no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 7,800/mm3, and platelet count 9,000/mm3. Peripheral smear shows isolated thrombocytopenia without schistocytes.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment to control bleeding and raise the platelet count?

answer_choices.text: Platelet transfusion alone
Plasmapheresis
High-dose corticosteroids with consideration of intravenous immune globulin
Observation with outpatient follow-up only
Packed red blood cell transfusion

questions.rationale: This patient has immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), suggested by isolated severe thrombocytopenia, mucocutaneous bleeding, a recent viral illness, and no evidence of hemolysis, infection, or splenomegaly. Because she has active mucosal bleeding and a platelet count of 9,000/mm3, initial treatment should include high-dose corticosteroids; intravenous immune globulin can be added when a rapid increase in platelets is needed to help control bleeding. This is the most appropriate initial therapy in the emergency department.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Platelet transfusion may be used as a temporizing measure for life-threatening bleeding, but transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed in ITP and transfusion alone is not adequate initial therapy.

Plasmapheresis is used for conditions such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, not isolated immune thrombocytopenia; this patient also lacks schistocytes, neurologic changes, renal injury, or hemolysis.

Observation alone is reasonable for some minimally symptomatic patients with higher platelet counts, but this patient has active mucosal bleeding and profound thrombocytopenia, so treatment is needed.
Packed red blood cells treat significant anemia or ongoing hemorrhage causing low hemoglobin, but this patient’s hemoglobin is normal and the primary issue is isolated thrombocytopenia.

questions.teaching_point: Symptomatic immune thrombocytopenia with mucosal bleeding is treated initially with corticosteroids, with intravenous immune globulin added when rapid platelet elevation is needed; platelet transfusion is reserved for severe or life-threatening bleeding as a temporary bridge.

questions.vignette: A 46-year-old woman presents to clinic because of intermittent numbness around her mouth and tingling in both hands over the past 2 weeks. She also reports occasional painful cramping in her calves and hands, especially when typing or carrying groceries. She had a thyroidectomy 3 months ago for multinodular goiter. She takes levothyroxine and a proton pump inhibitor. Vital signs are normal. On exam, she appears anxious but is alert and oriented. Strength is normal, but when she flexes her wrist during blood pressure cuff inflation, her hand develops painful flexion of the fingers and thumb within a minute.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding is most likely in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Proximal muscle weakness
Hyperreflexia with ankle clonus
Asterixis
Bradykinesia with cogwheel rigidity
Carpopedal spasm

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has symptomatic hypocalcemia, suggested by perioral paresthesias, distal tingling, muscle cramps, and a recent thyroidectomy that could have injured the parathyroid glands. The hand spasm induced by cuff inflation is a Trousseau-type response, and carpopedal spasm is a classic associated physical finding in hypocalcemia due to increased neuromuscular excitability.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Proximal muscle weakness is more characteristic of disorders such as hyperthyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica, or hypokalemia, rather than acute symptomatic hypocalcemia.

Hyperreflexia with ankle clonus suggests an upper motor neuron process or serotonin toxicity; although neuromuscular irritability can occur in hypocalcemia, this specific pattern is not the best associated finding here compared with carpopedal spasm.
Asterixis is a flapping tremor seen with metabolic encephalopathy, such as hepatic failure or severe hypercapnia, and does not fit this postoperative paresthesia and tetany picture.
Bradykinesia with cogwheel rigidity suggests Parkinson disease, which would not explain perioral tingling, hand cramps, or the cuff-induced hand spasm.

questions.teaching_point: Symptomatic hypocalcemia commonly causes perioral numbness, paresthesias, muscle cramps, and carpopedal spasm, especially after thyroid or parathyroid surgery.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: An 11-year-old boy with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes is brought to clinic for 3 weeks of worsening right ear pain and foul-smelling drainage. He has tried over-the-counter ear drops without improvement. His mother reports he now avoids chewing because it increases the pain. Exam shows swollen, tender external ear canal with granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction and mild tenderness over the mastoid. He is afebrile and otherwise well appearing.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment?

answer_choices.text: Incision and drainage of the external auditory canal
Reassurance that this is likely otitis media with effusion and will resolve spontaneously
Topical ciprofloxacin ear drops and dry ear precautions
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and a 7-day follow-up
High-dose oral ciprofloxacin with urgent ENT referral

questions.rationale: This child has malignant (necrotizing) external otitis, suggested by severe persistent otalgia, otorrhea, granulation tissue in the ear canal, and diabetes as a major risk factor. Management requires systemic antipseudomonal therapy because the infection can extend to the skull base; oral ciprofloxacin is appropriate for an outpatient who is stable, with urgent otolaryngology follow-up for further evaluation and monitoring. Topical therapy alone is inadequate.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Incision and drainage is not the treatment for necrotizing external otitis; the canal granulation reflects invasive infection rather than a drainable abscess.

Otitis media with effusion would not explain the severe progressive otalgia, foul drainage, and canal granulation tissue, and observation would inappropriately delay treatment of an invasive infection.

Topical fluoroquinolone drops are used for uncomplicated otitis externa, but this presentation has red flags for necrotizing external otitis and requires systemic treatment rather than topical therapy alone.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate does not provide reliable antipseudomonal coverage and is insufficient for necrotizing external otitis, which needs systemic therapy targeting Pseudomonas.

questions.teaching_point: Necrotizing external otitis in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient requires systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics and urgent ENT involvement; topical therapy alone is not enough.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 62-year-old woman comes to a walk-in clinic because of sudden pain in her right eye that began 2 hours ago while she was reading in a dim room. She reports blurred vision and sees halos around lights. She is nauseated and has vomited once. She has no history of eye trauma. She wears reading glasses only. On examination, the right eye is red with a mid-dilated, poorly reactive pupil, and the cornea appears hazy. Visual acuity is decreased in the affected eye.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding would be most consistent with this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Markedly elevated intraocular pressure on tonometry
Photophobia with a small, constricted pupil and ciliary flush
Mucopurulent discharge with lid crusting and chemosis
A branching dendritic lesion that stains with fluorescein
Painless sectoral loss of peripheral vision with a normal anterior chamber

questions.rationale: This patient has acute angle-closure glaucoma, suggested by sudden unilateral eye pain, blurred vision with halos, nausea/vomiting, a red eye, a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil, and a hazy cornea. A classic additional physical examination finding is markedly elevated intraocular pressure, which is best confirmed by tonometry. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency that requires immediate treatment to lower intraocular pressure and prevent permanent vision loss.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Photophobia, a small constricted pupil, and ciliary flush are more consistent with anterior uveitis. Uveitis can cause painful red eye, but it is not associated with the characteristic halos, hazy cornea, and markedly increased intraocular pressure of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Mucopurulent discharge, lid crusting, and chemosis are more typical of infectious conjunctivitis. Conjunctivitis usually causes irritation and discharge rather than severe eye pain, halos, a mid-dilated pupil, or elevated intraocular pressure.

A branching dendritic fluorescein-staining lesion is characteristic of herpes simplex keratitis. That condition can cause eye pain and redness, but it does not typically present with the sudden severe pain, halos, and markedly elevated intraocular pressure seen here.

Painless sectoral peripheral vision loss with a normal anterior chamber is more consistent with chronic open-angle glaucoma. That condition is usually gradual and asymptomatic until late, unlike the acute painful presentation described here.

questions.teaching_point: Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with sudden painful red eye, blurred vision with halos, nausea/vomiting, a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil, hazy cornea, and elevated intraocular pressure; it is an ophthalmic emergency.

questions.vignette: A 42-year-old woman is admitted with 2 days of fever, chills, nausea, and right flank pain. She has dysuria and urinary frequency. Vital signs are temperature 39.1 C (102.4 F), heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 108/68 mm Hg, and respirations 18/min. Exam shows costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis demonstrates positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, and pyuria.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study should be obtained before starting empiric antibiotics in this hospitalized patient with suspected acute pyelonephritis to identify the causative organism and guide therapy if needed?

answer_choices.text: Renal ultrasonography
Blood cultures
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Voiding cystourethrogram
Urine culture and sensitivity

questions.rationale: Urine culture and sensitivity should be obtained before antibiotics in a hospitalized patient with suspected acute pyelonephritis so the causative organism can be identified and antimicrobial therapy can be tailored if needed. Empiric antibiotics should then be started promptly; treatment should not be delayed while awaiting culture results.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Renal ultrasonography can assess for hydronephrosis or obstruction, but it does not identify the causative organism and is not the best initial diagnostic study before antibiotics in this presentation.

Blood cultures may be helpful if sepsis is suspected, but they do not replace urine culture for identifying the urinary pathogen and are not the most appropriate routine study before antibiotics in this case.
Contrast-enhanced CT is reserved for suspected complications such as obstruction, renal abscess, emphysematous infection, or failure to improve, not for routine initial evaluation before antibiotics.
Voiding cystourethrogram is used to evaluate vesicoureteral reflux, primarily in children, and is not part of the initial workup for adult pyelonephritis.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected acute pyelonephritis, obtain a urine culture before starting empiric antibiotics so therapy can be targeted to the organism and susceptibilities; do not delay treatment while waiting for results.

questions.vignette: A 10-month-old boy is admitted for episodic severe abdominal pain and vomiting. His parents report that he has been drawing his knees to his chest and crying for several minutes at a time, then appearing tired and briefly comfortable between episodes. Over the past day he has had decreased stool output, and this morning they noticed a small amount of bloody, mucus-like stool. On exam, he is irritable, the abdomen is soft between episodes, and a sausage-shaped mass is palpated in the right abdomen.
questions.lead_in: Which physical examination finding is most characteristic of this condition?

answer_choices.text: A palpable, elongated, sausage-shaped abdominal mass
A firm, mobile, epigastric olive-shaped mass
A palpable right upper quadrant mass with jaundice
Diffuse rebound tenderness with involuntary guarding
Localized right lower quadrant tenderness with a positive Rovsing sign

questions.rationale: Intussusception classically causes intermittent, severe, colicky abdominal pain in infants and may produce a palpable, elongated, sausage-shaped abdominal mass, often in the right abdomen. Bloody, mucus-like stool can also occur as bowel ischemia develops. The finding most characteristic on physical examination is the sausage-shaped mass.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A firm, mobile, epigastric olive-shaped mass is characteristic of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, not intussusception.
A right upper quadrant mass with jaundice suggests a hepatobiliary process or mass lesion, not intussusception.
Diffuse rebound tenderness and involuntary guarding suggest generalized peritonitis or bowel perforation, not the typical physical examination finding of intussusception.
Right lower quadrant tenderness with Rovsing sign is more consistent with appendicitis than intussusception.

questions.teaching_point: In infants, intussusception is suggested by episodic colicky abdominal pain, bloody mucus stool, and a palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD presents to urgent care with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and worsening shortness of breath that began while he was walking to his mailbox. He is speaking in short phrases but is alert. He has a 60-pack-year smoking history and uses home oxygen at night. Vital signs are BP 118/76 mm Hg, HR 112/min, RR 26/min, and SpO2 89% on his usual 2 L/min nasal cannula. Exam shows decreased expansion of the right chest, hyperresonance to percussion on the right, and markedly diminished breath sounds over the right hemithorax. He has no JVD, tracheal deviation, or hypotension. Portable chest radiograph confirms a moderate right apical pneumothorax without mediastinal shift.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Insert a small-bore chest tube with admission for monitoring
Discharge with oral analgesics and strict return precautions
Perform needle aspiration of the pleural space
Arrange outpatient pulmonology follow-up within 72 hours
Administer supplemental oxygen and observe with repeat imaging

questions.rationale: This patient has a symptomatic secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to severe COPD. In secondary pneumothorax, underlying lung disease means less pulmonary reserve and a lower tolerance for even a moderate pneumothorax. Because he is dyspneic, hypoxemic on supplemental oxygen, and has a moderate pneumothorax on imaging, the appropriate next step is hospital admission with pleural drainage using a small-bore chest tube. Observation alone is not appropriate, and needle aspiration is less reliable and generally not preferred for symptomatic secondary pneumothorax with significant lung disease.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Discharge without pleural intervention is unsafe because the patient remains symptomatic and hypoxemic, and secondary pneumothorax can worsen rapidly in patients with COPD.

Needle aspiration can be considered in selected stable spontaneous pneumothoraces, but in symptomatic secondary pneumothorax from COPD it is less reliable than chest tube drainage and is not the best next step here.
Outpatient follow-up alone is inappropriate for an actively symptomatic pneumothorax confirmed on imaging; immediate inpatient management is required.

Supplemental oxygen and observation are more appropriate for a small, minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax; this patient has a symptomatic secondary pneumothorax with limited cardiopulmonary reserve and needs drainage.

questions.teaching_point: Symptomatic secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in a patient with significant underlying lung disease usually requires inpatient pleural drainage rather than observation or outpatient management.

questions.vignette: A 42-year-old woman comes to clinic for episodic headaches and palpitations that have worsened over the past 4 months. During these spells, she feels sweaty, anxious, and tremulous. Her home blood pressure readings are often normal, but during an office visit last week they were 198/112 mm Hg. She also reports a 7-kg unintentional weight loss despite a normal appetite. She has no cough, fever, or stimulant use. Physical examination is normal between episodes. Her sister was recently diagnosed with a paraganglioma.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this patient's presentation?

answer_choices.text: Essential hypertension
Pheochromocytoma
Hyperthyroidism
Carcinoid syndrome
Panic disorder

questions.rationale: This patient has episodic headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, tremulousness, and paroxysmal severe hypertension, which are classic manifestations of catecholamine excess from pheochromocytoma. The normal examination between episodes is typical, and the family history of paraganglioma supports a hereditary catecholamine-secreting tumor syndrome. Although symptoms such as anxiety and weight loss can occur in other conditions, the combination of adrenergic spells and intermittent hypertension is most consistent with pheochromocytoma.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Essential hypertension may explain elevated blood pressure readings, but it does not account for episodic headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, and tremulous spells with normal intervals between episodes.
Hyperthyroidism can cause weight loss, tremor, and palpitations, but the episodic adrenergic spells and severe intermittent blood pressure elevations are more characteristic of pheochromocytoma.

Carcinoid syndrome typically causes flushing and diarrhea, sometimes with wheezing or palpitations, but it does not usually cause recurrent spells of severe hypertension with headaches and diaphoresis.

Panic disorder can cause palpitations, sweating, anxiety, and trembling, but it does not usually cause marked paroxysmal hypertension or a family history suggestive of a catecholamine-secreting tumor.

questions.teaching_point: Pheochromocytoma should be suspected when episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations occur with paroxysmal hypertension, especially when family history suggests a hereditary catecholamine-secreting tumor syndrome.

questions.vignette: A 16-year-old girl comes to an outpatient clinic requesting birth control. She is sexually active with one partner and wants a method she does not have to remember every day. She has regular menses, no history of migraine with aura, hypertension, clotting disorder, or liver disease. She does not smoke. Her mother is unaware of the visit. The patient says she would prefer a method that is highly effective and also helps make her periods lighter and less painful.
questions.lead_in: Which contraceptive method is the best recommendation for this patient?

answer_choices.text: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection
Copper intrauterine device
Etonogestrel subdermal implant
Combined oral contraceptive pills

questions.rationale: The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device is the best choice for an adolescent who wants a highly effective, low-maintenance contraceptive method. It requires little adherence, is safe for nulliparous adolescents, and commonly decreases menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea, matching her stated preferences. Compared with other highly effective methods, it is especially helpful when the patient also wants lighter, less painful periods.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is effective and does not require daily use, and it may reduce bleeding and dysmenorrhea in some patients. However, it is less ideal here because it is associated with weight gain and reversible bone mineral density loss, and the levonorgestrel IUD is a better fit for her overall preferences.
The copper IUD is highly effective and low-maintenance, but it can increase menstrual bleeding and cramping, making it a poor fit for a patient who wants lighter, less painful periods.

The etonogestrel implant is highly effective and low-maintenance, but it does not reliably improve menstrual bleeding patterns and can cause unpredictable bleeding, which makes it less ideal for a patient who specifically wants lighter, less painful periods.
Combined oral contraceptive pills can improve menstrual pain and bleeding, but they require daily adherence, which conflicts with her desire not to remember a method every day.

questions.teaching_point: For adolescents who want highly effective, low-maintenance contraception, long-acting reversible contraception is first-line. The levonorgestrel IUD is especially useful when the patient also wants decreased menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea.

questions.vignette: A 28-year-old graduate student presents to an outpatient clinic with 9 days of gradually worsening cough, low-grade fever, headache, and fatigue. She says the cough began dry and is now intermittently productive of small amounts of sputum. She has no dyspnea at rest, chest pain, or wheezing. She recently recovered from a mild sore throat and nasal congestion, and several classmates have had similar “walking pneumonia” symptoms. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 92/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Lung examination reveals scattered faint expiratory crackles at the bases without focal decreased breath sounds or egophony.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding would be most consistent with this patient’s likely illness?

answer_choices.text: Diffuse, fine inspiratory crackles with mild pharyngitis and a generally unimpressive chest examination
Localized bronchial breath sounds with egophony and dullness to percussion over one lower lobe
Unilateral wheezing that improves immediately after bronchodilator administration
Markedly decreased tactile fremitus with hyperresonance on one side
High-pitched stridor with suprasternal retractions and drooling

questions.rationale: Mycoplasma pneumonia commonly causes an atypical outpatient pneumonia in younger adults with a gradual onset of constitutional symptoms, dry cough, mild pharyngitis, and relatively subtle chest findings that may include diffuse, faint crackles rather than focal lobar consolidation. The vignette’s age group, exposure history, subacute course, and minimal focal lung findings fit this pattern.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Localized bronchial breath sounds, egophony, and dullness to percussion suggest lobar bacterial pneumonia with alveolar consolidation, which is more focal and typically more abrupt than the presentation here.
Unilateral wheezing that responds to bronchodilator therapy is more consistent with asthma or reactive airway disease than an atypical pneumonia syndrome with constitutional symptoms and crackles.

Decreased tactile fremitus with hyperresonance on one side suggests pneumothorax, which would usually present with sudden pleuritic chest pain and acute dyspnea rather than a gradual flu-like illness.
Stridor, retractions, and drooling indicate upper airway obstruction such as epiglottitis or severe laryngeal pathology, not a lower respiratory tract atypical infection.

questions.teaching_point: Mycoplasma pneumonia often presents in adults with a gradual, flu-like illness, dry cough, and mild or diffuse lung exam findings rather than focal consolidation.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is admitted for progressive fatigue, mild confusion, and worsening arthralgias. His family reports darkening of his skin over the past year and decreasing exercise tolerance. He has type 2 diabetes and newly recognized cirrhosis on abdominal ultrasound obtained during the admission. Labs show hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, ferritin 1,680 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 84%, and elevated AST/ALT. Genetic testing confirms HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis. He is hemodynamically stable, has no active bleeding, and his hemoglobin/hematocrit are adequate for treatment.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Begin serial therapeutic phlebotomy
Start deferoxamine chelation therapy
Transfuse packed red blood cells
Administer intravenous iron replacement
Observe and repeat ferritin in 6 months

questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis with markedly elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation, plus adequate hemoglobin and hemodynamic stability. The first-line treatment is serial therapeutic phlebotomy to remove excess iron and reduce the risk of progression to cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, diabetes complications, and other end-organ damage. In a stable patient without anemia, phlebotomy is the appropriate immediate intervention.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Iron chelation is generally reserved for patients who cannot undergo phlebotomy, such as those with transfusion-related iron overload or significant anemia. It is not first-line for uncomplicated hereditary hemochromatosis.
Packed red blood cell transfusion is not indicated because the patient is not anemic or unstable. Transfusion would add additional iron and exacerbate the condition.
Intravenous iron would worsen iron overload and is contraindicated in a patient with confirmed hemochromatosis and markedly elevated iron indices.
Observation alone is inappropriate because the patient already has biochemical iron overload and evidence of organ involvement. Delaying treatment increases the risk of irreversible complications.

questions.teaching_point: Hereditary hemochromatosis with adequate hemoglobin is treated first-line with serial therapeutic phlebotomy to lower iron stores and prevent organ damage.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman presents to an outpatient clinic with 2 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, and new left flank pain. She reports subjective fever and nausea but has been able to drink fluids. She is nonpregnant and has no history of kidney stones, urinary tract obstruction, recurrent urinary infections, or immunocompromise. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 102/min. Costovertebral angle tenderness is present on the left. A urine dipstick in the office is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study should be obtained before starting antibiotics to identify the causative organism and guide therapy?

answer_choices.text: Urine culture and sensitivity
Blood cultures
Noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Cystoscopy
Renal ultrasonography

questions.rationale: Urine culture and sensitivity should be obtained before antibiotics when possible in suspected acute pyelonephritis. The diagnosis is usually made clinically with urinalysis support, and the urine culture identifies the causative organism and antibiotic susceptibilities so therapy can be tailored if needed.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Blood cultures are reserved for patients with severe illness, sepsis, hospitalization, or suspected bacteremia. They are not the routine preantibiotic diagnostic study for uncomplicated outpatient pyelonephritis.

Noncontrast CT is most useful when nephrolithiasis or obstruction is suspected. This patient has an uncomplicated presentation of pyelonephritis, so CT is not the routine study needed before treatment.
Cystoscopy evaluates the bladder and lower urinary tract and is not used to diagnose or guide treatment of an acute upper urinary tract infection such as pyelonephritis.

Renal ultrasonography is not routinely required for uncomplicated acute pyelonephritis. It is mainly used when obstruction, hydronephrosis, or another structural abnormality is suspected, or in pregnancy.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected uncomplicated acute pyelonephritis, obtain a urine culture before antibiotics whenever possible; imaging is reserved for suspected obstruction, stones, pregnancy, severe illness, or failure to improve.

questions.vignette: A 46-year-old man is found on routine labs to have elevated ferritin and increased transferrin saturation. He reports fatigue and mild arthralgias but has no acute symptoms. He is newly diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis and asks about treatment to reduce his iron burden.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial outpatient intervention?

answer_choices.text: Defer treatment until liver biopsy confirms cirrhosis
Therapeutic phlebotomy
Immediate packed red blood cell transfusion
Iron chelation therapy with deferoxamine as first-line treatment
Dietary iron restriction alone without other therapy

questions.rationale: Therapeutic phlebotomy is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated hereditary hemochromatosis in a stable outpatient. Regular removal of blood lowers total body iron stores and helps prevent organ injury. Treatment should not be delayed pending liver biopsy unless there is a specific concern for advanced liver disease or diagnostic uncertainty.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Treatment should begin once iron overload is identified; waiting for biopsy-proven cirrhosis delays effective therapy and is not necessary in an otherwise stable outpatient.
Packed red blood cell transfusion adds iron and is reserved for symptomatic anemia or acute blood loss, neither of which is present here.

Iron chelation is generally reserved for patients who cannot undergo phlebotomy, such as those with severe anemia or other contraindications, and is not first-line for uncomplicated hereditary hemochromatosis.
Dietary iron restriction alone does not adequately remove excess iron stores and is not sufficient as sole therapy for hereditary hemochromatosis.

questions.teaching_point: Hereditary hemochromatosis is treated first with therapeutic phlebotomy to lower iron stores and prevent end-organ injury.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 1 day of fever, severe headache, photophobia, and vomiting. On examination, he is confused, has neck stiffness, and his temperature is 39.4°C (103°F). Blood cultures and lumbar puncture are obtained, and the cerebrospinal fluid is grossly cloudy with neutrophilic predominance, elevated protein, and low glucose.
questions.lead_in: Which cerebrospinal fluid finding is most characteristic of acute bacterial meningitis?

answer_choices.text: Xanthochromia
Oligoclonal bands
Decreased glucose concentration
Lymphocytic predominance
Normal protein concentration

questions.rationale: Acute bacterial meningitis typically produces a cerebrospinal fluid profile with low glucose due to bacterial and neutrophil metabolism, along with elevated protein, elevated opening pressure, and neutrophilic pleocytosis. In this patient, the cloudy CSF and neutrophil predominance are classic for a bacterial process, making decreased CSF glucose the characteristic finding.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Xanthochromia suggests prior subarachnoid hemorrhage or blood breakdown products in CSF, not acute bacterial meningitis.
Oligoclonal bands are associated with demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis, not acute bacterial meningitis.
Lymphocytic predominance is more typical of viral meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, or other chronic inflammatory conditions rather than acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis.
CSF protein is usually elevated in bacterial meningitis because of inflammation and increased blood-brain barrier permeability, not normal.

questions.teaching_point: Acute bacterial meningitis classically causes cloudy CSF with neutrophils, low glucose, and elevated protein.

questions.vignette: A 10-year-old girl is brought to clinic because of 4 months of worsening fatigue, intermittent abdominal pain, and decreased appetite. Her mother reports that the child has lost weight despite eating normally at first and has become increasingly irritable. She has had several episodes of dizziness when standing and now avoids gym class because she feels weak. On exam, her blood pressure is 86/54 mm Hg, pulse is 108/min, and she appears thin. Mild diffuse darkening of the skin is noted on the gums and creases of the palms. Mild generalized weakness is noted, but her neurologic exam is otherwise normal. The family says she has not started any new medications and has no history of steroid use.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this patient’s presentation?

answer_choices.text: Type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis
Primary adrenal insufficiency due to autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex
Hyperthyroidism causing weight loss and tachycardia
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Central adrenal insufficiency due to pituitary ACTH deficiency

questions.rationale: This child has primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease): progressive fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain, decreased appetite, orthostatic dizziness, hypotension, weakness, and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. In primary adrenal failure, cortisol deficiency leads to increased pituitary ACTH production, and ACTH shares melanocyte-stimulating activity, causing skin darkening. Autoimmune adrenalitis is a common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in children, but the diagnosis here is based on the clinical syndrome; further testing would be needed to determine the exact etiology.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Type 1 diabetes can cause weight loss and fatigue, but this vignette lacks polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, Kussmaul respirations, or acute metabolic illness. It also does not explain hyperpigmentation or persistent orthostatic hypotension.

Hyperthyroidism can cause weight loss, irritability, and tachycardia, but it would more typically include heat intolerance, tremor, and goiter rather than orthostatic hypotension, abdominal pain, and hyperpigmentation.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency can present with adrenal insufficiency and hyperpigmentation, but it usually begins earlier in life and is often associated with virilization, precocious puberty, or a history of ambiguous genitalia or salt-wasting crises.

Central adrenal insufficiency can cause fatigue, weight loss, and hypotension, but ACTH is low or inappropriately normal, so hyperpigmentation is not expected. Aldosterone secretion is usually preserved, making marked salt-wasting less typical.

questions.teaching_point: Primary adrenal insufficiency in children should be suspected when fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain, orthostatic symptoms, hypotension, and hyperpigmentation occur together; elevated ACTH in primary disease causes skin darkening.

questions.vignette: A 42-year-old woman comes to clinic because of 8 months of fatigue, constipation, weight gain despite no change in diet, and increased sensitivity to cold. She also reports dry skin and heavier menstrual periods. On exam, her heart rate is 56/min, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and her thyroid feels diffusely enlarged, firm, and nontender. She has mild periorbital puffiness and delayed relaxation of the deep tendon reflexes.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis
Thyroid carcinoma
Graves disease
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Toxic multinodular goiter

questions.rationale: This patient has classic features of primary hypothyroidism in an adult, including fatigue, constipation, weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia, dry skin, menorrhagia, delayed relaxation of reflexes, and a diffuse, firm, nontender goiter. Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas and commonly presents with these findings.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Subacute thyroiditis is typically painful and tender and often follows a viral illness; it more often causes a transient thyrotoxic phase before hypothyroidism.
Thyroid carcinoma usually presents as a solitary thyroid nodule or mass, sometimes with compressive symptoms, rather than diffuse hypothyroid symptoms and a symmetric firm goiter.
Graves disease causes hyperthyroid symptoms such as heat intolerance, weight loss, tachycardia, tremor, and often ophthalmopathy rather than bradycardia and hypothyroid features.
Toxic multinodular goiter causes hyperthyroidism with an irregularly enlarged thyroid and symptoms of excess thyroid hormone, not the diffuse firm goiter and hypothyroid picture seen here.

questions.teaching_point: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in adults and presents with hypothyroid symptoms plus a diffuse, firm, nontender goiter.

questions.vignette: A 67-year-old postmenopausal woman is admitted for worsening abdominal distention and early satiety over the past 4 months. She reports vague pelvic pressure and decreased appetite but no fever, vomiting, or change in bowel habits. Exam shows a distended abdomen with a shifting dullness. Pelvic examination reveals a firm, irregular adnexal mass. She has no history of cirrhosis or heart failure. Abdominal CT demonstrates ascites and a complex pelvic mass with nodular peritoneal implants.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma
Endometrial hyperplasia
Uterine leiomyoma
Benign ovarian cyst
Pelvic inflammatory disease

questions.rationale: This postmenopausal patient has progressive bloating, early satiety, ascites, a complex adnexal mass, and peritoneal implants, which are classic findings of advanced epithelial ovarian carcinoma. Ovarian cancer often presents with vague, nonspecific abdominal or pelvic symptoms and is commonly diagnosed after spread beyond the ovary.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia typically presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in peri- or postmenopausal patients, rather than an adnexal mass with ascites.
Uterine leiomyomas can cause heavy menstrual bleeding or bulk symptoms, but they are less likely to present with ascites and peritoneal implants in a postmenopausal patient.
A benign ovarian cyst may be asymptomatic or cause mild pelvic discomfort, but ascites and nodular peritoneal implants are concerning for malignancy rather than a benign lesion.

Pelvic inflammatory disease usually causes pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, and infectious symptoms, and it would not explain a complex adnexal mass with peritoneal implants in this clinical context.

questions.teaching_point: In a postmenopausal patient, vague abdominal symptoms plus an adnexal mass and ascites should raise strong concern for epithelial ovarian cancer.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 74-year-old man is admitted after falling forward onto the edge of a coffee table. He has right periorbital swelling, diplopia when looking upward, and numbness over the right cheek. Visual acuity is unchanged from baseline, pupils are equal and reactive, and there is no afferent pupillary defect. Extraocular movements are limited in upgaze on the affected side, and there is mild tenderness over the orbital floor. He is not taking anticoagulants. The trauma team is concerned about an orbital wall injury with possible entrapment.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected injury and define its extent?

answer_choices.text: MRI of the orbits with contrast
Bedside ocular ultrasonography
Plain radiographs of the facial bones
Noncontrast CT scan of the orbits and maxillofacial bones
Fluorescein staining with slit-lamp examination

questions.rationale: Noncontrast CT of the orbits and maxillofacial bones is the best study for suspected orbital blowout fracture because it accurately identifies orbital wall fractures, herniation of orbital contents, and extraocular muscle entrapment. In a patient with diplopia, upgaze limitation, and infraorbital numbness after blunt trauma, CT is the preferred imaging test to define bony injury and guide surgical consultation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: MRI is not the initial study for acute orbital trauma because it is slower, less available, and inferior to CT for defining bony fracture anatomy.
Bedside ocular ultrasonography can help assess posterior segment pathology in some eye complaints, but it does not adequately evaluate orbital wall fractures or muscle entrapment.
Plain facial radiographs are less sensitive than CT for orbital floor fractures and provide inadequate detail about subtle bony defects and soft tissue entrapment.
Fluorescein staining with slit-lamp examination is useful for corneal abrasion or globe surface injury, but it will not confirm an orbital fracture or assess the bony extent of trauma.

questions.teaching_point: Suspected orbital blowout fracture is best evaluated with noncontrast CT of the orbits/maxillofacial bones, especially when diplopia, restricted upgaze, or infraorbital numbness suggests entrapment.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is in an inpatient rehabilitation facility 10 days after a mechanical fall that caused a small left subdural hematoma managed nonoperatively. He has hypertension and atrial fibrillation and was taking apixaban before the fall, which was held on admission. Over the past 24 hours, he has become increasingly sleepy and has had a new right foot drag during therapy. He now has a mild right pronator drift and slowed speech. Vital signs are stable. His head CT today shows a left crescent-shaped extra-axial collection that is larger than on prior imaging with a 6-mm midline shift.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Observe in the rehabilitation unit and repeat neurologic checks in 24 hours
Hold anticoagulation and arrange routine outpatient follow-up in 1 week
Restart apixaban at full dose to reduce the risk of cardioembolic stroke
Administer hypertonic saline and continue inpatient rehabilitation without further escalation
Transfer the patient urgently to a higher level of care and obtain emergent neurosurgical consultation

questions.rationale: This patient has neurologic deterioration after a known subdural hematoma, with new focal deficits, worsening somnolence, interval enlargement of the collection, and midline shift. These findings indicate clinically significant mass effect and possible need for operative evacuation. The appropriate next step is urgent escalation to a higher level of care and emergent neurosurgical consultation. Further rehabilitation-level observation or delayed follow-up is unsafe, and anticoagulation should not be restarted in the setting of an enlarging intracranial hemorrhage.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Observation in the rehabilitation unit is unsafe because the patient has objective neurologic worsening and imaging evidence of progression with midline shift.

Routine outpatient follow-up is inappropriate because this patient has a worsening neurologic exam and CT evidence of expanding subdural hematoma with midline shift, which requires urgent inpatient escalation.
Restarting anticoagulation now would increase the risk of further intracranial bleeding in a patient with an enlarging hemorrhage and new mass effect.

Hypertonic saline can be a temporizing measure for elevated intracranial pressure, but it does not replace urgent transfer and neurosurgical evaluation when a subdural hematoma is enlarging and causing new neurologic deficits.

questions.teaching_point: New neurologic deficits or declining mental status after subdural hematoma, especially with enlarging collection or midline shift, require urgent neurosurgical escalation.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man with a history of metastatic lung cancer presents to the emergency department with 2 days of worsening shortness of breath, chest pressure, and lightheadedness. He was discharged from chemotherapy 1 week ago after a recent pleural effusion was drained. On arrival, he is anxious and sitting upright. Vital signs show blood pressure 88/56 mm Hg, heart rate 124/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Neck veins are distended, heart sounds are muffled, and the lungs are clear bilaterally. The radial pulse weakens noticeably during inspiration. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRS complexes. He is too unstable to leave the resuscitation area for advanced imaging.
questions.lead_in: Which immediate diagnostic study should be performed first to confirm the diagnosis and assess for hemodynamic compromise?

answer_choices.text: Chest radiography
Computed tomography angiography of the chest
Electrocardiography with serial repeat tracings
Focused bedside cardiac ultrasound (transthoracic echocardiography)
Serum troponin measurement

questions.rationale: This patient has hypotension, jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, and low-voltage ECG findings, which strongly suggest cardiac tamponade causing obstructive shock.
