Her parents also want to know what should be addressed before discharge to reduce the chance of relapse and medical complications after she leaves the hospital. The patient is receiving a multidisciplinary inpatient eating-disorder program.
questions.lead_in: Which discharge planning element is most important to reduce relapse and medical complications after discharge?

answer_choices.text: Discontinue all family involvement to promote autonomy and reduce conflict around meals
Schedule regular weight, vital sign, and growth-curve monitoring with outpatient eating-disorder follow-up after discharge
Focus follow-up care only on psychotherapy because medical monitoring is unnecessary once refeeding begins
Delay outpatient follow-up until the patient reaches her premorbid weight
Recommend immediate return to unrestricted sports participation once vital signs normalize

questions.rationale: Adolescents hospitalized for anorexia nervosa need structured discharge planning with close outpatient monitoring of weight, vital signs, growth trajectory, and eating-disorder symptoms. Because relapse and medical instability are common after discharge, ongoing medical surveillance and coordinated specialty follow-up are essential to reduce morbidity. Return to sports should remain restricted until the patient is medically stable, weight restored, and cleared through follow-up assessment.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Family involvement is often a key part of treatment in pediatric anorexia nervosa. Removing family support can worsen adherence to nutritional rehabilitation and increase relapse risk.

Medical monitoring remains necessary after refeeding because adolescents remain at risk for relapse, bradycardia, hypotension, and other complications. Psychotherapy alone is not sufficient after hospitalization.

Waiting until premorbid weight is reached before arranging follow-up is too late and increases the risk of deterioration after discharge. Follow-up should begin immediately with close outpatient monitoring.

Return to unrestricted athletics is unsafe before adequate weight restoration and sustained medical stability are documented. Normalization of a few inpatient vital signs does not mean the patient is ready for full sports participation.

questions.teaching_point: After inpatient stabilization for pediatric anorexia nervosa, discharge planning should include early outpatient eating-disorder follow-up and regular monitoring of weight, vitals, and growth to prevent relapse and medical complications.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 34-year-old woman comes to clinic because her 3-year-old son was recently diagnosed with retinoblastoma. The child’s pediatric oncologist confirms a germline RB1 mutation. The mother reports that her own father lost an eye to an unknown childhood cancer, and she is unsure whether anyone in the family ever had genetic testing. Her 6-month-old daughter has no eye symptoms and had a normal newborn exam. The mother asks what should be done now to protect her daughter from a similar cancer.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management for the infant daughter?

answer_choices.text: Arrange urgent genetic counseling with targeted RB1 testing for the infant and immediate dilated ophthalmologic examination/surveillance while testing is being completed
Schedule only a routine well-child follow-up visit because a normal newborn exam rules out hereditary retinoblastoma
Reassure the family that the infant does not need evaluation unless she develops leukocoria or strabismus
Order orbital ultrasonography as the initial screening test for the asymptomatic infant instead of an eye examination
Obtain parental RB1 testing first and wait for those results before any evaluation of the infant

questions.rationale: This infant is at increased risk for hereditary retinoblastoma because her sibling has retinoblastoma with a confirmed germline RB1 mutation. The most appropriate next step is urgent genetic counseling with targeted testing for the known familial RB1 variant, along with immediate ophthalmologic surveillance using dilated eye examination while genetic results are pending. Early eye screening is important because retinoblastoma may be asymptomatic initially and can progress quickly, so management should not wait for symptoms or for genetic confirmation before ophthalmic evaluation begins.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A normal newborn exam does not exclude hereditary retinoblastoma, and routine pediatric follow-up alone is inadequate for an infant with this degree of genetic risk.
Observation until symptoms develop is inappropriate in a high-risk infant. Retinoblastoma may not cause early symptoms, and delayed evaluation can miss a treatable tumor.
Ultrasonography is not the preferred initial screening approach for an asymptomatic high-risk infant. The key next steps are genetic counseling/testing and prompt dilated ophthalmologic surveillance.
Parental testing is not required before evaluating the infant when a familial RB1 mutation is already known in the affected sibling. Waiting delays risk assessment and necessary surveillance.

questions.teaching_point: When a child has retinoblastoma with a confirmed germline RB1 mutation, at-risk siblings need prompt genetic counseling, targeted familial variant testing, and immediate dilated ophthalmologic surveillance rather than watchful waiting.

questions.vignette: A 63-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 3 days of worsening left flank pain and one episode of gross hematuria. He has a 30-pack-year smoking history and is being evaluated for unintended 8-kg weight loss over the past 4 months. Vital signs are stable. Exam shows left costovertebral angle tenderness and a palpable fullness in the left upper abdomen. Urinalysis confirms hematuria without pyuria or nitrites. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast shows a 7-cm enhancing left renal mass extending into the left renal vein, with no hydronephrosis. His pain is controlled with IV opioids, and his hemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Start empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and admit for presumed acute pyelonephritis
Place a ureteral stent to relieve presumed obstructive uropathy
Discharge the patient with oral analgesics and outpatient follow-up in 6 months
Arrange urgent urologic consultation for nephrectomy and vascular surgical evaluation
Administer tissue plasminogen activator for suspected renal vein thrombosis

questions.rationale: This patient has imaging findings highly concerning for renal cell carcinoma with local extension into the renal vein, which can cause hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable mass. In the ED, the appropriate next step is urgent specialty consultation for definitive surgical management, typically radical nephrectomy with evaluation of venous involvement. He is hemodynamically stable, has no evidence of infection or urinary obstruction requiring immediate decompression, and the CT has already identified a surgically significant renal mass.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pyelonephritis is unlikely because he lacks fever, pyuria, nitrites, and systemic signs of infection, and CT demonstrates a solid enhancing renal mass rather than an infectious process.

Ureteral stenting is used to relieve obstructive uropathy from collecting system obstruction, but his CT shows no hydronephrosis and his symptoms are explained by a renal mass with venous extension rather than ureteral obstruction.

Although outpatient oncologic follow-up is needed, this is not an appropriate delayed-disposition case because the CT shows an advanced renal mass with venous invasion that requires urgent urologic evaluation rather than routine follow-up.
Renal vein involvement here is from tumor extension, not acute thrombotic disease. Thrombolysis is not indicated and would be dangerous in a patient with active hematuria and a renal malignancy.

questions.teaching_point: A symptomatic enhancing renal mass with hematuria and renal vein invasion is renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise and warrants urgent urologic surgical consultation.

questions.vignette: A 52-year-old woman is admitted for treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. During medication reconciliation, she reports that she takes an oral contraceptive pill daily for birth control and also likes that it regulates her bleeding. She has had increasingly infrequent menses over the past 2 years, with her last menstrual period 9 months ago. She is in a monogamous relationship and asks whether she can stop the pill after discharge because she thinks she may be nearing menopause. Her blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, and she has no history of venous thromboembolism, stroke, or breast cancer.
questions.lead_in: Which counseling statement is the most appropriate?

answer_choices.text: She should switch immediately to a copper intrauterine device because oral contraceptives are contraindicated once menstrual cycles become irregular.
She should stop contraception permanently because pregnancy is no longer possible after age 50.
She should continue contraception until menopause is confirmed or until age 55 if menopause cannot be confirmed.
She should check a serum follicle-stimulating hormone level while continuing the pill to determine whether she is menopausal.
She can stop contraception now because 9 months without menses confirms menopause.

questions.rationale: This patient is perimenopausal, not yet confirmed to be postmenopausal. Menopause is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhea in the absence of another cause. Because she is 52 and has had only 9 months without menses, she may still ovulate and can still become pregnant. In a healthy, nonsmoking woman without estrogen contraindications, combined oral contraceptives can be continued during the menopausal transition, and contraception should generally be continued until menopause is confirmed or, if it cannot be confirmed, until about age 55 when spontaneous conception becomes exceedingly unlikely. The pill may also help with bleeding control during this transition.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Irregular menses alone is not a contraindication to combined oral contraceptives. A copper intrauterine device is an option, but an immediate switch is not required solely because she is perimenopausal.
Pregnancy is still possible after age 50, although fertility declines. Contraception should not be stopped solely because she has passed age 50.

Follicle-stimulating hormone testing while continuing combined oral contraceptives is not a reliable way to determine menopausal status because hormonal contraception suppresses gonadotropins and can obscure interpretation.
Nine months of amenorrhea does not confirm menopause. Menopause is defined after 12 consecutive months without menses, assuming no other cause.

questions.teaching_point: Perimenopausal women may still need contraception; menopause is confirmed after 12 months of amenorrhea, and if menopause cannot be confirmed, contraception is generally continued until about age 55 in otherwise eligible patients.

questions.vignette: A 13-year-old girl is brought to an urgent care clinic by her mother for sudden left lower abdominal pain that began 4 hours ago while she was at cheerleading practice. The pain is severe, constant, and associated with nausea and one episode of vomiting. She had a similar but milder episode yesterday that improved after resting. Her last menstrual period was 10 days ago, and she denies vaginal bleeding, dysuria, diarrhea, or fever. She has not been sexually active. On exam, she appears uncomfortable and pale. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), heart rate is 112/min, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Abdomen is soft with focal tenderness in the left lower quadrant without rebound or guarding. Pelvic examination is deferred because of age and discomfort. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.
questions.lead_in: Which additional historical feature or physical finding would most increase concern for the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Crampy lower abdominal pain that begins with the onset of menses and improves with NSAIDs
Fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, and cervical motion tenderness
Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain that improves within a few hours and then recurs later in the day
Pain that localizes to the right lower quadrant and is associated with anorexia and rebound tenderness
Gradual onset of bilateral lower abdominal pain with dysuria and urinary frequency

questions.rationale: Intermittent, severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting is classic for adnexal torsion, which may involve twisting and untwisting of the ovary. In an adolescent with sudden focal lower abdominal pain and vomiting, a history of recurrent episodes that temporarily resolve would further increase concern for ovarian torsion and the need for urgent gynecologic evaluation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pain that begins with menses and improves with NSAIDs is more consistent with primary dysmenorrhea, which causes recurrent menstrual cramping rather than sudden unilateral pain with nausea and vomiting.

Fever, malodorous discharge, and cervical motion tenderness suggest pelvic inflammatory disease or another infectious process, which is less likely in a pre-/early-adolescent patient who has not been sexually active and does not fit the abrupt presentation.

Right lower quadrant pain with anorexia and rebound tenderness is more suggestive of appendicitis, which can mimic pelvic pain but does not classically cause intermittent unilateral pelvic pain that resolves and recurs.
Gradual bilateral pain with dysuria and urinary frequency suggests a urinary tract infection or cystitis, which typically causes urinary symptoms rather than sudden focal pelvic pain and vomiting.

questions.teaching_point: Adnexal torsion in adolescents classically presents with sudden unilateral pelvic pain and nausea/vomiting, sometimes with intermittent episodes from twisting and untwisting; it requires urgent evaluation to preserve ovarian function.

questions.vignette: A 24-year-old woman comes to an outpatient clinic because of 8 months of progressive weight loss and fatigue. She reports strict calorie counting, daily exercise, and frequent weighing. Her body mass index is 16 kg/m2. She has not had a menstrual period for 7 months. On exam, she has dry skin, lanugo-like fine hair on her forearms, and mild bradycardia. The clinician is evaluating the medical complications associated with her suspected eating disorder.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is most appropriate to assess a common chronic complication of this condition related to bone health?

answer_choices.text: Plain radiograph of the wrist
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan
Electrocardiogram
Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone level

questions.rationale: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scanning is the most appropriate study to assess bone mineral density. Anorexia nervosa is commonly associated with low bone density and osteoporosis because of malnutrition and hypoestrogenism, especially in patients with prolonged amenorrhea. In this patient, DEXA is the best test to evaluate this chronic complication.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A plain radiograph of the wrist can detect an acute fracture, but it is not used to screen for the low bone mineral density common in anorexia nervosa.
A serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level may identify a contributing nutritional deficiency, but it does not directly evaluate bone density or diagnose osteoporosis.
An electrocardiogram can evaluate bradycardia or conduction abnormalities in anorexia nervosa, but it does not assess bone mineral density, which is the complication targeted here.
Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone level may be checked in the evaluation of weight loss or endocrine symptoms, but it does not assess the chronic bone-related complication of anorexia nervosa.

questions.teaching_point: In adults with anorexia nervosa and prolonged amenorrhea, DEXA scanning is used to evaluate for osteopenia and osteoporosis, common chronic complications of low estrogen and malnutrition.

questions.vignette: A 28-year-old man is admitted after surgical repair of an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection. He has a tall, thin habitus, long fingers, pectus deformity, and a history of lens dislocation. His postoperative course is uncomplicated, and he is preparing for discharge. He asks what long-term measure is most important to reduce the risk of future cardiovascular complications. He takes no chronic medications and has no known drug allergies.
questions.lead_in: Which recommendation is the most appropriate preventive management to lower his future risk of aortic events?

answer_choices.text: Avoid strenuous isometric exercise and heavy lifting, but no further cardiovascular follow-up is needed
Start losartan alone and stop blood pressure monitoring after discharge
Schedule transthoracic echocardiography only if he develops chest pain or dyspnea
Repeat aortic imaging only once in 5 years if his postoperative blood pressure remains normal
Begin lifelong beta-blocker therapy and arrange regular surveillance imaging of the aortic root and ascending aorta

questions.rationale: This patient has Marfan syndrome and has already suffered an acute type A aortic dissection, placing him at very high risk for recurrent aortic enlargement, dissection, and aneurysm formation. Long-term management requires reduction of aortic wall stress with lifelong beta-blocker therapy and ongoing surveillance imaging of the aortic root and ascending aorta. Blood pressure should continue to be monitored, and an angiotensin receptor blocker may be used as adjunctive therapy in some patients, but it should not replace beta-blockade and serial imaging after dissection repair.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Avoiding heavy isometric exercise is appropriate counseling, but it is insufficient by itself. He also needs lifelong medical therapy and regular imaging follow-up to reduce recurrent aortic risk.

Losartan may be helpful in Marfan syndrome, but monotherapy and stopping blood pressure monitoring are not appropriate after a repaired aortic dissection, when beta-blockade and continued surveillance are needed.

Imaging only when symptoms develop would miss silent progression of aortic dilation or aneurysm formation. Patients with Marfan syndrome and prior dissection require scheduled surveillance rather than symptom-triggered testing.

Waiting 5 years for repeat imaging is far too infrequent after repaired type A dissection. Early and serial aortic surveillance is necessary because recurrent dilation or dissection can occur without symptoms.

questions.teaching_point: After aortic dissection in Marfan syndrome, lifelong beta-blockade plus serial aortic imaging are key preventive measures; exercise restriction alone is not enough.
